Then the covenant text itself: in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. It matters enormously where that sentence comes from. It is spoken on a mountain in Genesis 22, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught by its horns in a thicket — the promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham's line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided, and no ram was found, and the knife was not stopped. Abraham got his boy back down the mountain. God did not spare his own.

And then the last sentence, which is where the whole chapter has been going. God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.

Take the two halves in turn. To you first — in the city that killed him, to the crowd that asked for a murderer instead, the offer arrives before it goes anywhere else in the world. That is the pattern of the whole book, to the Jew first, city after city, long after the doors start closing. And it is a window onto the character of God, who deals with the people who have wronged him worst by putting them at the front of the queue.

Then the definition. To bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness. Peter states outright what the blessing consists of, and it is not what most people mean by the word. Ask a room of ordinary people what a blessing is and the answers will be about health, safety, provision, children doing well, a scan that came back clear. Ask a congregation and the answers will be much the same with a religious accent laid over them. Here is an apostle, at the climax of a sermon, defining the blessing promised to Abraham for the entire world — and it is being turned away from your own wickedness.

That deserves a test. Suppose a man were given a long life and an easy one, comfortable, well provided for, with every person he loves kept safe — and suppose he arrived at the end of it exactly as he began, still governed by the temper, the appetite, the coldness or the dishonesty he has had since he was twenty. Was he blessed? By the definition in this verse he was never touched. And suppose another man loses most of what he owned and half of what he hoped for, and is prised loose over thirty years from the thing that was quietly destroying him. Peter says God blessed the second one.

Which is the note this chapter ends on, and it is worth hearing for what it says about God. He does not send his Servant to a crowd of murderers with a bribe, an amnesty, or a fresh start on the same old terms. He sends him to change them — to take hold of the people who killed him and turn them round, one at a time, every one of you. The man at the gate asked for a coin and was given his legs. Israel asked for a Messiah who would deal with the Romans and was offered something far more expensive and worth incalculably more: to be turned, personally, out of their own wickedness, by the one they had nailed to a cross.

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. “His name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong” (v. 16). This verse is not about a formula but about a person. The name in the ancient world carried the authority and presence of the one who bore it. When Peter speaks the name of Jesus, he is not invoking magic; he is acting in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ. The healing is an act of the risen Lord performed through his servant. Faith is the hand that reaches for what the name offers. And what the name offers is the full power of the one who conquered death — resurrection life, flowing through a living faith, into a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth, set daily at the gate of the temple he could not enter, excluded by his condition from the presence he longed for. His whole life had been one long reaching-out of an empty hand. And then, in the name of Jesus, he entered the temple walking.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. No program, no therapy, no government initiative can do what the name of Jesus does — not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and to offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were glorifying God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The Sadducees are annoyed. They have tolerated a great deal, but the resurrection — they cannot have the resurrection preached in the temple courts. For the Sadducees, resurrection is not just wrong theology; it is a direct challenge to their authority. So they arrest Peter and John. But it is too late: five thousand have believed. The arrest comes after the harvest. This is the pattern in Acts: the Word goes out, the kingdom grows, the opposition rises — and the opposition never wins.

The next morning Peter stands before the same council that tried Jesus. He is not the same Peter. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he does not hedge, does not soften, does not negotiate. He gives them the name: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. And then the sentence that has stopped every comfortable ecumenism in its tracks: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” The council marvels. They cannot deny the miracle — the healed man is standing right there. They can only warn. And Peter and John go back to the church and they pray.

The prayer is worth lingering over. They do not pray for safety. They do not pray for the opposition to relent. They pray for boldness. And the place is shaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The gospel's first opposition comes not from Gentile pagans but from the Jerusalem religious establishment — the priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees. Their problem is not with Peter's miracle but with Peter's preaching: the proclamation of resurrection in Jesus cuts directly against Sadducean theology and threatens the temple hierarchy's authority. They arrest the apostles, hold them overnight, and convene the full council of rulers, elders, and scribes — the same body that had condemned Jesus — to interrogate them the next morning.

What follows is one of the most remarkable scenes in Acts. Before the greatest concentration of religious power in Jerusalem, two unlettered Galilean fishermen speak with a clarity and courage that astonishes the council. Peter's defense is not a defense at all — it is a proclamation. 'This Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.' Exclusive, absolute, unembarrassed. The Spirit promised for persecution (Luke 12:11–12) has arrived.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exclusivity of Christ

Peter's declaration in v. 12 — 'there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved' — is one of the clearest statements of Christ's exclusive salvific lordship in all of Scripture. Reformed theology has always insisted on this exclusivity as a corollary of the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, in one particular place, at one particular time, then salvation is tied to that particular person. Plurality of saviors would require plurality of incarnations, which contradicts the logic of the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter and John were uneducated laymen standing before the supreme court of Israel. Their boldness astonished the council, who recognized that 'they had been with Jesus.' Now: The same Spirit who gave Peter and John their courage and clarity is given to every believer. The boldness to speak the name of Jesus in hostile contexts is not a personality trait — it is the Spirit's gift to those who ask (v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary: The opposition comes while Peter is still speaking — the authorities cannot wait for the sermon to end. The annoyance is specifically theological: Sadducean theology denied resurrection (Acts 23:8), and the apostles are proclaiming resurrection as the central fact of the gospel. Every sermon Peter preaches is simultaneously a refutation of the Sadducean worldview. The religious establishment's stake in the status quo is threatened not by miracles but by the message that interprets them: Jesus rose, and his resurrection overturns their entire system.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary: The arrest cannot stop the word already spoken: 'many of those who had heard the word believed.' The gospel operates faster than the authorities can respond. Five thousand men now believe — the church that began with 120 in an upper room has grown exponentially in days. The pattern is established here and will repeat throughout Acts: opposition and growth run together. The more the authorities attempt to suppress the message, the more rapidly it spreads. Human authority cannot arrest a word that has already taken root in human hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary: The full weight of Jewish institutional authority is assembled: Annas (the power behind the high priesthood, the patriarch of the priestly clan), Caiaphas (who had prophesied that one man should die for the people, John 11:50), and all who belonged to the high-priestly family. This is the same Sanhedrin that had condemned Jesus to death. The concentration of religious, political, and social power facing two Galilean fishermen is absolute. And it will prove entirely insufficient against the Spirit who fills them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By what power or by what name?' — the council asks precisely the right question, which is also the central question of the entire book of Acts. Everything turns on the name and the authority behind it. They expect the name to expose a source they can discredit and a power they can dismiss. What they receive instead is the most complete and uncompromising christological declaration they could have imagined — spoken with a boldness that leaves them no room to maneuver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by whom he was healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Filled with the Holy Spirit' — this is the fulfillment of Jesus's promise in Luke 12:11–12: 'when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.' Peter is not reciting a prepared speech; he is speaking as the Spirit gives utterance. And he begins with a rhetorical inversion: the council has framed this as an interrogation, but Peter immediately reframes it — they are being examined for 'a good deed.'

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary: The answer to 'by what name?' is given without hesitation or diplomacy: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised. Both facts — the human guilt of the crucifixion and the divine act of the resurrection — are stated directly to the people most responsible for both. The citation of Psalm 118:22 applies the builder-and-stone metaphor directly to the council: they are the builders who rejected the stone, and God has made that rejected stone the cornerstone of the entire edifice of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most exclusive and most comprehensive statement in Acts — and one of the most contested in the history of the church. Exclusive: salvation is in no one else; no other name. Comprehensive: 'under heaven,' 'given among men,' 'by which we must be saved' — the scope is universal and the necessity is absolute. This is not arrogance but logic: if God became flesh in one particular person, and if that person died and rose for the salvation of the world, then salvation is tied to that person. The incarnation itself entails the exclusivity of Christ (cf. John 14:6; 1 Tim. 2:5).

This is also one of the great apologetic verses, for the world calls it narrow and arrogant: how can Jesus be the only way? Three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation simply is found in him and nowhere else — not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way (one Saviour), infinitely wide in the welcome ('whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,' Rom. 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save — a man can be sincerely wrong, as one who sincerely drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker. As for those who never hear, Scripture's answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Rom. 1:20), none seek God on their own (Rom. 3:11), the Judge of all the earth will do right (Gen. 18:25) — and therefore we must go and tell ('how are they to hear without someone preaching?' Rom. 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deut. 29:29). (Others soften the exclusivity — pluralism says all religions are valid paths; inclusivism says some may be saved through Christ without conscious faith in him. The historic and Reformed position is that salvation is through Christ alone, received by conscious faith in him, normally through the gospel preached.) Far from cruel, this is the most loving truth there is: if Jesus really is the only Saviour, then telling people is the kindest thing we could ever do.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they could say nothing against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They had been with Jesus' — the council's observation is the most accurate commentary on what they are witnessing. The boldness (parrēsia) of Peter and John is not natural confidence — it is the quality that comes from having spent three years with the Son of God and now being filled with his Spirit. The healed man standing beside them is the unanswerable argument: you cannot refute a walking miracle. The council's problem is not lack of evidence; it is the will to suppress the evidence they have.

The council's own description is worth getting right, since it is often misheard. Uneducated does not mean illiterate; the word means without formal training in the rabbinic schools — no letters after the name. And common men renders a word for laymen, private persons, amateurs as opposed to professionals. The Sanhedrin is not saying that Peter and John cannot read. It is saying they have no credentials: they have not sat at the feet of a Gamaliel, as the young Saul of Tarsus had.

This is not an argument against learning — Luke writes careful Greek, Paul was thoroughly trained, and the church has needed both kinds of men ever since. It is a note about where the power was not coming from. The council looked for a qualification that would explain what they were seeing, found none on paper, and then named the real one without meaning to: they had been with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary: The council's private deliberation is a remarkable document of suppressed conscience: 'We cannot deny it.' The evidence is undeniable; the miracle is public knowledge; the healed man is standing in the room (v. 14). The problem is not lack of evidence — it is the will to believe. Their question 'What shall we do with these men?' is the same question the crowd at Pentecost asked from genuine openness (2:37); here it is asked from the desire for containment. The difference between saving faith and hardened unbelief is not the evidence available but the posture of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The strategy is containment rather than refutation: suppress the name, stop the spread. The council understands that the power of the apostolic ministry lies entirely in the name of Jesus — remove the name, and the movement (they hope) will collapse. Their charge is sweeping: 'not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.' They are asking the apostles to do the one thing that the apostles regard as a divine obligation. The collision between human command and divine commission is now absolute.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter and John's response is the first and most ringing statement of Christian civil disobedience in history. They do not argue, threaten, or negotiate; they simply state the impossibility of compliance: 'whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge.' The judgment is submitted to the council's own conscience, which must know the answer. And then the personal statement: 'we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.' Eyewitnesses of the resurrection cannot be made to act as if they have not seen what they have seen (cf. Acts 5:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were glorifying God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary: The council is constrained by the people's response: all Jerusalem is glorifying God for the healing of a man who has been lame for more than forty years. Political fear defeats theological hostility — the authorities cannot punish men the public regards as heroes without losing their own influence. Luke's note about the man's age underscores the magnitude of the miracle: forty years of lameness, instantaneously and completely healed. There is no natural explanation. The council knows it, the people know it, and the apostles are free — for now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Peter and John return to their community and report what the council has said, the church does the only thing it knows to do: it prays. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is one of the most theologically rich prayers in the New Testament — a model of how the church addresses God in the face of hostility. It begins with God as sovereign Creator, grounds itself in the fulfillment of Psalm 2 in the crucifixion, and asks not for protection from suffering but for boldness to continue the mission and signs to confirm it. The church that prays this way is the church that the Spirit fills and the world cannot stop.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God and Human Responsibility

The prayer of 4:27–28 is one of the most explicit statements of divine sovereignty in Acts: 'Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel,' did 'whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.' The crucifixion is the supreme demonstration that God's plan is not thwarted by human wickedness but accomplished through it. Reformed theology sees here the foundation of confidence in mission: if God can use the greatest evil in history (the murder of his Son) for the greatest good (the salvation of the world), no opposition can ultimately frustrate his purposes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church shared everything — not because the apostles commanded it, but because the Spirit had filled them with love. Barnabas selling his field is the named example of an unnamed pattern throughout the community. Now: The Spirit-filled community is always a generous community. The test of genuine spiritual vitality is not the excitement of meetings but the openness of hands.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The apostles' first act on release is not strategy but prayer — returning to the community and lifting up the community's voice to God. 'Sovereign Lord' (despota) — not the polite 'Lord' (kyrios) but the absolute master with total authority over all he has made. The prayer begins with creation: before they address their immediate crisis, they anchor themselves in the most fundamental truth — the God who made everything is the God they are addressing. The council's threats, framed against the backdrop of the Creator's sovereignty, look very small.

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation of Psalm 2 is inspired: the psalm describes the nations raging against God and his anointed, which is exactly what the council is doing. The church is reading the present situation through Scripture and finding that God has been here before — and won. The rulers gathered against the Lord's Anointed in Jerusalem two thousand years after Psalm 2 was written are simply repeating the pattern the psalm describes. The God who laughs at the nations' vain plotting (Psalm 2:4) is the God the church is addressing. They are praying from the winning side.

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary: The cross is named as the supreme example of human opposition meeting divine sovereignty: every party (Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, Israel) gathered against Jesus, and every action they took was simultaneously their free choice and God's predestined plan. The prayer does not explain the mystery; it simply affirms both realities side by side. And the church draws courage from this: if God's hand and plan governed the crucifixion, then his hand and plan govern the present opposition too. Nothing that happens to the church is outside his sovereignty (cf. Isa. 53:10; Luke 22:22).

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer's request is remarkable for what it does not ask: it does not ask for the threats to stop, for the council to relent, or for protection from suffering. It asks for boldness to speak in the face of threats, and for the continued manifestation of God's healing power through the name of Jesus. The church's request is more mission than the authorities have threatened to suppress. This is the prayer posture of a community that has fully transferred its security from earthly protection to divine empowerment.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary: God answers the prayer for boldness by filling them again with the Spirit who produces boldness. The physical shaking of the building is a theophanic sign — the presence of the divine response to prayer, recalling the earthquake at Sinai and the shaking of Isaiah's temple vision (Isaiah 6:4). The answer is immediate and unmistakable: the place shakes, the Spirit fills, and they speak the word of God with boldness. The boldness they asked for is the gift the Spirit gives, and the Spirit's gift is the answer to the prayer for the Spirit's gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One heart and soul' (kardia kai psychē mia) — the deepest unity imaginable: a community of shared will and desire. This is what the Spirit produces in people who are fully yielded to him. The economic sharing flows from the spiritual unity: when people genuinely share one heart, the sharing of possessions follows naturally. 'With great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection' — the community's internal life of unity and generosity is the context in which the external proclamation of resurrection gains its credibility and its power (cf. John 17:21–23).

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was not a needy person among them' — the church fulfills the Deuteronomic vision (Deuteronomy 15:4, 'there will be no poor among you') not by compulsion but by generosity. The laying at the apostles' feet and distribution according to need creates a community that embodies the kingdom's economics: from those who have, freely given; to those who lack, justly supplied. The apostles' role as distributors of the community's resources is temporary — the appointment of the Seven in ch. 6 will formalize a better arrangement — but the principle of need-driven generosity is permanent.

A word here, since this is sometimes called 'Christian communism' and pressed into political service: it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary — Peter tells Ananias, 'while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?' (5:4) — so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was love-driven and Spirit-prompted, flowing from hearts made 'one,' not enforced by any state. And it was needs-based generosity ('as any had need'), not mechanical equalising. This is the very opposite of coercive collectivism: it is the free, glad open-handedness of people whom the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment's response.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke names Barnabas as the positive example of the community's generosity — the named illustration of an unnamed pattern. Barnabas ('son of encouragement') will reappear throughout Acts as the man who consistently sees potential where others see danger (9:27, 11:25–26, 15:39). His generosity here is the first glimpse of a character that will prove essential to the Gentile mission. The Levite who cannot own land in Israel (Numbers 18:20) but owns a field in Cyprus gives it away — his belonging is no longer to the tribe but to the community of the risen Christ.

4.theology: The Sovereignty of God and Mission. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is a theology lecture compressed into seven verses. God is addressed as despotēs — Sovereign Lord, absolute Master — who made heaven and earth and everything in them. Herod and Pilate and the nations, in their opposition to Christ, did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.” This is not fatalism; it is the Reformed doctrine of providence applied to history’s darkest moment. And the implication for mission is not paralysis but boldness: if God was sovereign over the crucifixion, he is sovereign over every threat to the gospel. The church does not need favourable conditions to advance the kingdom. It needs the Spirit and the Word. God provides both.
4.examples:
Then: A church five weeks old, under arrest, before the same council that crucified their Lord, with no legal protection, no political allies, no plan B — and they prayed for boldness and were given it. The shaking of the place was God’s receipt: prayer received, boldness granted.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same fork: silence or speech, safety or boldness. The prayer of Acts 4 is still available. The God who shook that room has not grown quiet. He is still the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And he still grants boldness to those who ask for it — not because they deserve it, but because his Word must go out.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter passed his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council and all the senate of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, and they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we did not find anyone inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
Two things happen in Acts 5 that seem to pull in opposite directions — and both are necessary. Ananias and Sapphira fall dead for lying to the Holy Spirit. And the apostles are beaten and leave the council rejoicing. The fear of God and the joy of the Lord are not opposites; they are the two poles of a life lived before the face of the Holy One. A church that has lost one will eventually lose both.

The sin of Ananias and Sapphira is not that they kept some of the money. Peter makes this explicit: the money was theirs to keep. The sin is the performance — the pretence of complete consecration while secretly holding back. They lied to the Holy Spirit. The God who fills his church with his presence will not be managed or deceived within his own house. The result: great fear came upon the whole church. This is the fear that is the beginning of wisdom. The church needed it then. The church always needs it.

Then the apostles are beaten. And they leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name. This is not stoicism; this is the freedom of those who have been so captured by the worth of Christ that physical suffering has become, in the light of his glory, a privilege they are grateful to share.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The story of Ananias and Sapphira is the most disturbing episode in the early chapters of Acts, and it is meant to be. Luke has just introduced Barnabas, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet; he opens this chapter with a but and two people who did the identical thing for the opposite reason. They do not steal from the community. They lie to it — keeping part of the proceeds while presenting the whole as a gift. The sin is not the retention; Peter says plainly that the money was theirs to keep (v. 4). The sin is the performance of a consecration they had privately declined to make. Luke even signals it in his vocabulary: the verb for what they kept back is the one used of Achan hiding plunder in his tent as Israel entered the land.

The judgement falls twice, three hours apart, and both times the apostle only says aloud what is already true; Peter pronounces no sentence and claims no power. Sapphira is given a question she could have answered honestly and gives the rehearsed answer instead. Both are buried within the hour, without mourning. And what Luke records as the outcome is not horror but fear — great fear on all who heard, and then on the whole church, which he now calls the church for the first time in the book. The severity is a mercy to the community: a people whose whole life rested on the assumption that when a Christian speaks it is so, protected at the outset from those who had discovered the assumption could be exploited.

Then, immediately, the second half of the section, and the two halves belong together. Signs and wonders are done regularly by the apostles' hands; the believers gather openly in Solomon's Portico, the most public religious space in Jerusalem, not hidden away. Nobody on the fringe dares attach himself casually any more — and in the same breath more than ever believers are added to the Lord, multitudes of men and women. The city begins carrying the sick into the streets so that Peter's shadow might fall on them, and people come in from the surrounding towns with the sick and the demonised, and they are healed. This is the pattern Luke wants seen: the fear did not empty the church, it purified it, and the purified church was the one the Spirit filled and the city could not stay away from.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Holiness of God and the Danger of Hypocrisy

The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira stand in a recognisable biblical pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood (Leviticus 10), Achan at Israel's entry into the land (Joshua 7), Uzzah as the ark comes home (2 Samuel 6), and here the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgements — one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once. They are not the rule; God's ordinary way is the patient kindness meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), which is precisely why the rest of us are still breathing. A God who never enforced his own holiness would not be holy, and the gospel does not lower that holiness but satisfies it, so that those in Christ may come near to the Holy One with confidence. The second half of the section shows what such a God does with a church that has learned to tremble before him: he fills it, and multiplies it, and heals through it in the open street.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church five weeks old discovered that the Spirit who filled it also searched it — and that the same fear which drove off the hangers-on drew in multitudes.

Now: The pattern repeats wherever religious performance stands in for reality: the testimony allowed to run better than the facts, the prayer that warms when others are listening, the struggle described in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. Two cautions belong with it. This chapter is not a lever for extracting money — Peter says the field and the proceeds were theirs. And the fear here came from what God did, not from what the leaders did; a congregation frightened of its elders has reproduced what this chapter killed, not what it created. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything depends on the word Luke opens with. But. The paragraph before this one introduced a Levite from Cyprus called Joseph, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, son of encouragement, who sold a field and laid the money at their feet (4:36–37). Luke names him, and then immediately names two other people who did the identical thing and were not the same at all. He has set them side by side deliberately. The outward act was indistinguishable. Same field sold, same walk across the room, same money on the same floor.

And then the verb, which is where this story actually begins. The word for kept back is nosphizomai, and it is not a common one. Outside this chapter the New Testament uses it once, of household slaves pilfering from their masters (Titus 2:10). But in the Greek Old Testament it turns up at one unforgettable place: Joshua 7:1, where Achan takes for himself some of what had been devoted to God at Jericho, hides it in his tent, and stands in the assembly the next morning as though nothing had happened, while Israel is defeated at Ai and nobody knows why. That is not an echo a reader has to strain for. Luke has reached for Achan's own word. Israel had just crossed into the land and the first sin inside the new order was a private theft concealed in public; the church has just crossed into its own new order, and here it is again, in the same vocabulary.

Notice what they were actually buying, because it was not money. They could have kept the whole field and sinned in nothing. They could have sold it and given a tenth openly and been thanked. What they wanted was something the honest options could not supply: the reputation of total surrender, at a price they had negotiated down in private. Barnabas had gone from a nobody to a name in one afternoon, and it is the easiest thing in the world to want that and to want it cheaply. So they arranged an appearance. The laying of the money at the apostles' feet was a public gesture in front of a watching room, and the gesture was the whole point. They did not steal from the church. They bought applause with counterfeit currency and had it accepted at face value.

And it was not a moment's weakness. With his wife's knowledge — Luke will not let that pass, and Peter will come back to it (v. 9). Two people sat down together, discussed a figure, agreed what they would say, and rehearsed a story well enough that she could still deliver it three hours after he was dead. Every private sin has a moment where it could have been stopped by one person saying no. This one had two people in the room and neither of them said it. The marriage that should have been the safest place for an honest word became the place where the lie was made airtight.

Before anyone comforts himself that this is an extreme case, measure it against the ordinary version. The testimony that is allowed to stand a little better than the facts warrant. The prayer that lengthens and warms when other people are listening. The reply 'we've been praying about that' when the last time you prayed about it was in March. The struggle described to a small group in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. None of that is a felony, and none of it is what Ananias did on the scale he did it. But it is the same transaction. It is buying a reputation for a devotion you have not got, and paying in a currency you know to be false.

One thing must be guarded before the passage goes any further, because this chapter has been misused for money more often than almost any other. It is not a warning about giving too little. Peter will say in two verses that the field was theirs and the proceeds were theirs and no one had any claim on either. A church that produces Ananias and Sapphira to loosen a congregation's grip on its wallet has inverted the passage exactly: the sin here was not withholding, it was pretending, and the pressure to perform generosity is nearer to what killed them than the withholding ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's Spirit-given discernment exposes the sin at once: not the retention of money (entirely their right — 'while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?') but the lie — presenting part as whole, a generosity they were not practicing.

'Why has Satan filled your heart…?' — Peter means it really and personally: Satan genuinely instigated the sin. The verb 'filled' (eplērōsen) is the dark mirror of being 'filled with the Spirit' (Acts 2:4; 4:8, 31; cf. Eph. 5:18) — which means not a warm feeling but to be so wholly taken up and governed by God that his presence controls one's words and courage. Here the same word runs the other way: Satan floods and masters Ananias's heart, so that his tongue and deed are ruled toward a lie. This sets Ananias beside Judas, into whom 'Satan entered' to betray Jesus for money (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Behind the deceit stood the personal adversary, striking the newborn church from within at the very hour the gospel advanced with power (the echo of Achan, whose secret sin defiled Israel at the threshold of the land, Josh. 7, is not merely in the reader's ear — Luke has put it into the vocabulary; see on vv. 1-2).

Yet Satan's hand is no excuse. In the same breath Peter asks, 'Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart?' (v. 4): both are true at once — Satan filled his heart, and Ananias schemed it in his own. Scripture holds these together everywhere (Luke 22:3 beside Luke 22:22; Gen. 50:20; Acts 2:23): the tempter does not override the will but inflames a heart already willing. As James says, 'each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire' (James 1:14) — Ananias's lie fed on his own covetousness and craving for praise, and Satan fanned the flame. 'The devil made me do it' is no excuse, and Peter offers none.

Is every sin, then, a special act of Satan like this? Scripture sets the proportions. Lying in particular bears his family likeness, for Jesus calls him 'a liar and the father of lies' who 'speaks out of his own character' (John 8:44) — which is why his hand is so visible here; and in a broad sense all sin serves his kingdom (Eph. 2:2; 1 John 3:8). But the ordinary spring of sin is the human heart itself — 'out of the heart of man come evil thoughts… deceit' (Mark 7:21–23) — not, as here and with Judas, a direct 'filling' by Satan. The old shorthand names three sources working together — the world, the flesh, and the devil — all three of which Paul gathers in a breath (Eph. 2:2–3): the 'course of this world,' the 'prince of the power of the air,' and 'the passions of our flesh.' The world is not the created order or the people God loves, but the whole system of human life organized against him, its values and applause pulling the heart away (1 John 2:15–16; James 4:4); the flesh is not the body but the fallen self, the inward bent toward sin we carry from Adam, warring against the Spirit (Gal. 5:16–17; Rom. 8:7). Behind and through both the devil works — so we neither blame every sin on demons nor pretend he has no hand in it.

And through it all Ananias remains fully responsible: 'you have not lied to man but to God.' The Spirit dwelling in the church is the living God himself, so to deceive his people is to lie to him ('you are God's temple and God's Spirit dwells in you,' 1 Cor. 3:16). Where the text is silent we will not pretend — Luke says Satan filled the heart and Ananias contrived the deed, but not how that 'filling' worked. We rest in what is revealed: real satanic instigation, real human guilt, no excuse, and a holy God who is not mocked (Gal. 6:7). For the heart of their sin was an attempt to deceive God — to parade a lie of wholehearted devotion before the One who reads the heart, as though he could be fooled; and to try to fool God is to mock him. He saw through the performance, and judged it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice where Luke puts the weight. He does not linger over Ananias; he tells us the effect: 'great fear came upon all who heard.' That is the point of the scene. The death is unannounced — Peter pronounces no sentence, he only exposes the sin; it is God's response, not Peter's punishment — and its result is a church that suddenly grasps whom it is dealing with. The Spirit among them is no benevolent force that winks at religious play-acting; he is the holy God himself.

Why so severe, when nearly every liar walks away still breathing? Because Scripture shows a pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness — Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood (Lev. 10:1–2), Achan at Israel's entry into the land (Josh. 7), Uzzah as the ark comes home (2 Sam. 6:6–7), and here the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgments — one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once to stamp God's holiness on his people and to keep a young, tender church from being poisoned at its core. 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified' (Lev. 10:3): nearness to God raises the demand for reverence, it never lowers it.

Then why do the rest of us not fall dead at every lie? Because these are the exception, not the rule. God's ordinary way is patient kindness, meant to lead us to repentance (Rom. 2:4; Ps. 130:3), and one Ananias, recorded forever, teaches the whole church age — the lightning flashes once to light up the whole landscape. And for the believer the deepest answer is the cross: the judgment our sin deserves has already fallen on Christ. So the fear Luke records is not the terror that drives us from God but the awe that keeps us from trifling with him — the reverence of a people who have seen, close up, that their God is holy (cf. 5:11).

Verse 6 is easy to read past and should not be. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. Four verbs, no pause, and no funeral. In a Jewish household a death set in motion days of formal mourning — the tearing of clothes, the wailing, the seven days of visitors, the family shut in with its grief. None of that happens. He is wrapped where he fell and in the ground before the sun has moved far, and the ordinary marks of respect for the dead are simply not given. Luke reports it without comment, which is itself a comment. The church did not stage a scandal, did not hold an inquiry, and did not honour him. It buried him, quietly and fast, and there is something more sobering in that plain sentence than in the death itself. And the men who carried him out came back, and three hours later were still there, and had to do it a second time.

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three hours. Luke times it, and the interval is the most merciful stretch of Sapphira's life. Somewhere in the city she is going about an ordinary afternoon, and her husband has been dead since before lunch, and nobody has come to tell her. Then she walks in through the door, not knowing what had happened, into a room where every person present knows exactly what has happened and what she is about to say.

Watch what Peter does, because it matters enormously and it is almost always missed. He does not accuse her. He does not tell her that her husband is dead, and he does not say what he already knows. He asks a question, and he makes it as easy to answer truthfully as a question can possibly be made: tell me whether you sold the land for so much. There is no trap in it. It is a door held open. One sentence — no, actually it was more than that, and we said otherwise — and this entire episode ends with a woman in tears and a church learning about forgiveness instead of about judgement. God did not spring the trap on her. He gave her the last three hours and then he gave her the question.

Yes, for so much. Two words in the Greek, and they are the sound of a rehearsed line. She does not hesitate, does not glance round the room, does not ask why she is being asked. She has the figure ready because they had agreed the figure. And notice the pressure she was not under: her husband was not standing beside her. Nobody was watching her to see whether she would hold the line. She could have broken the agreement at no cost to a marriage that had, unknown to her, already ended. She kept it anyway, alone, freely, which is precisely why Peter's next words treat her as a principal and not as a wife who was dragged along.

That raises something this passage speaks to directly, and it is worth saying plainly because women have been badly counselled about it. A wife is nowhere in Scripture required to follow her husband into sin, and a husband's headship has never included the authority to make a liar of her. The point is not obscure: it is the same principle the apostles will state to the highest court in the land later in this very chapter — we must obey God rather than men (v. 29). If that holds against a Sanhedrin, it holds against a husband, and it holds in a kitchen. Scripture actually gives the picture: Abigail went round her husband's ruinous folly, acted without his knowledge to stop it, and is commended for it in the text and by David himself (1 Samuel 25). Sapphira had the same road available and did not take it. Her tragedy is not that she submitted; it is that she agreed.

There is a particular kind of sin that only two people can commit, and this is it. A shared lie is far more durable than a private one, because each partner is now the other's evidence that it is not so bad. Neither has to face it alone, and so neither ever faces it. Whatever conversation Ananias and Sapphira had in the days before this one, it ended with both of them steadier in the deception than either would have been by himself. Three hours were given to break it, and she spent them keeping her side of the bargain.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her answer is still in the air when Peter names what she has done, and he names it as a partnership. You have agreed together. The verb is symphoneo, to sound together, the word behind our symphony — two instruments in tune. It is one of the loveliest things about a marriage, that two people can come to one mind about something without needing to argue it out, and here it is, working perfectly, in the service of a lie. Whatever else was wrong in that house, they were not at odds. They had harmony. They had used it to make the deception airtight.

And what they had agreed to do, Peter says, was to test the Spirit of the Lord. That phrase unlocks the whole episode, and it is worth being exact about it, because the English word misleads. Testing here has nothing to do with examining whether something works, the way a man tests a rope before he trusts his weight to it. The word (peirazo) means to put God to the proof — to presume on him, to dare him, to find out whether he is really watching and will really act. Israel did it at Massah, demanding water and asking, is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:2; Psalm 95:9). It is the one temptation Jesus refused outright on the temple pinnacle, quoting the law back at the tempter: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16; Matthew 4:7). Ananias and Sapphira had, in effect, laid a wager that the Spirit would not notice, or would notice and not mind. They were not sceptics; they had watched the Spirit fall and had seen the healings. They simply did not believe he was paying attention to them. They found that he was.

Then Peter tells her something that no husband should ever have to be told by a stranger, and he tells it in the same breath as her own sentence: the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door. She learns she is a widow and that she is about to follow him, in one sentence, standing up, in front of a room. It is worth insisting again on what Peter is and is not doing here. He pronounces no penalty. He passes no sentence. He has no power to strike anybody and he does not claim any; he is reporting, the way a man reports weather he can see coming. The judgement in this chapter is God's, twice, and both times the apostle only says out loud what is already true.

Luke's last detail is the one that ought to be felt. She fell down at his feet. Go back seven verses and see where she last stood in this room: her husband laid the money at the apostles' feet (v. 2). That was the whole object of the exercise — that square of floor, the public gesture, the watching room. It is the exact spot where she falls. The place they had wanted to be seen is the place she is carried from.

And then the young men come back in, and do again what they had done three hours earlier, and she is buried beside him. Together in the planning, together in the rehearsing, together in the ground. Luke does not moralise over it and the tidiness of his sentence is more frightening than any commentary could be. As for why this sin, and her husband's, met so immediate a judgement when sin is not ordinarily repaid on the spot, see on vv. 5-6: God's normal way is patient forbearance meant to lead to repentance, and this is the exception recorded once so that it need not be repeated.

It is right to find the passage terrible. It would be wrong to find it arbitrary. God was not defending his dignity against an insult; he was defending a five-week-old church against the one thing that kills churches from the inside, which is people who have learned to perform a devotion they do not have and to be admired for it. Everything the early chapters describe — the one heart and soul, the goods held loosely, the apostles' teaching received as the word of God — depends on the assumption that when a Christian says a thing, it is so. Two people set out to prove that assumption could be exploited. The Lord of the church answered in a way that meant nobody tried it again for a very long time.

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twice now Luke has stopped the narrative to tell us the effect rather than the event — great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5), and now great fear came upon the whole church. He is not reporting an atmosphere in passing. He is telling us what the episode was for. And he adds a second circle: and upon all who heard of these things. It did not stay indoors. Jerusalem heard, and Jerusalem drew its own conclusions about what sort of company this was.

Notice, too, the word he chooses at this exact moment. This is the first time in Acts that Luke calls the believers the church (ekklesia). Not at Pentecost, with the wind and the fire and the three thousand. Not in the golden paragraph about having all things in common. Here — in the silence after two funerals, in a room that has just learned what it is living with. To be the church is, before anything else, to reckon with the holiness of the God who has moved in.

And this fear is not the enemy of the church's life; it is the soil of it. Watch what grows in the next three verses: signs and wonders, a people all together in Solomon's Portico, and more than ever believers added to the Lord, multitudes of men and women. The awe did not freeze the church. It purified it and then filled it. A community that takes God seriously is one the Spirit is pleased to inhabit and the watching world is drawn to — sobered and attracted at the same moment, which is a combination no institution has ever been able to manufacture.

For this is not cringing terror that runs from God, nor the thin modern 'respect' that trembles at nothing, but reverent awe that draws near in love and yet will not trifle — the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Picture a man at his hearth on a winter night. He loves the fire, pulls his chair as close as he can bear, and would not dream of putting his hand into it, because he knows perfectly well what it is. He is not afraid of the fire in the sense of wanting to be further from it. He is nearer to it than anyone else in the house. That is the fear of the Lord, and Luke will later name it as the very mark of a healthy church: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit (9:31). Both, in one sentence, without embarrassment.

Something has to be said, though, to the reader who has finished this passage and cannot settle. There is a particular person who reads Acts 5 and lies awake — who knows he is not what he appears to be in his church, who can name the exaggeration and the unconfessed thing, and who now half expects the floor to open. That fear deserves a straight answer rather than a soothing one. Ananias was not caught out by a God waiting to pounce; he engineered a lie in the presence of God over a period of days, with a partner, and was given a question at the end of it that he could have answered honestly. So was she. Neither of them wanted to be found out; both of them wanted to be admired more than they wanted to be true. A man who is trembling because he longs to be genuine and knows he is not yet is describing an entirely different condition, and the trembling itself is the evidence. The Spirit does not produce that ache in people he is about to strike down. He produces it in people he is not going to leave alone. And the door out of it is open and has always been open: say the true thing, to God first and then to whoever needs to hear it, and the whole weight of it goes.

What Ananias and Sapphira had lost was precisely this fear, and it is possible to lose it in a room full of miracles. The church, seeing them lose it, learned it. That is the mercy hidden in the hardest paragraph in Acts: two people were the last to learn what the whole church learned that day, and everyone else got it for nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Signs and wonders' — the words reveal their purpose. A 'sign' (sēmeion) points beyond itself; a 'wonder' (teras) astonishes. They were never ends in themselves but meant to authenticate the message and its messengers — God's seal on the apostolic gospel. Scripture says so: the miracles were 'the signs of a true apostle' (2 Cor. 12:12); God 'bore witness' to the gospel 'by signs and wonders and various miracles' (Heb. 2:3–4); the Lord 'confirmed the message by accompanying signs' (Mark 16:20) and granted 'signs and wonders to be done by their hands' (Acts 14:3); even Jesus' signs were written 'so that you may believe' (John 20:31). The wonder was the wrapping, the word the gift — which is why Jesus rebuked those who craved signs for their own sake (Matt. 12:39).

This authenticating purpose is why the historic Reformed church has held that these apostolic sign-gifts have ceased — a case drawn from Scripture, not mere observation. The signs marked out the apostles (2 Cor. 12:12), and the apostles were a foundation laid once: the church is 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets' (Eph. 2:20), and a foundation is laid only once. Their office could not be handed on (its men had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ; Paul is 'last of all,' 1 Cor. 15:8), and the revelation those signs authenticated is complete — 'the faith once for all delivered' (Jude 3). Once the foundation was laid and the message set in Scripture, the credentials that attested the foundation-layers had served their purpose, like scaffolding taken down once the building stands.

Two honest qualifications. First, no verse says outright, 'miracles will cease when the apostles die.' The certain ground is the purpose of the signs; the timing of their ceasing is a strong inference from that purpose joined to the close of the apostolic age and the completed canon — not a single proof-text (1 Cor. 13:8–10 does say tongues and prophecy will 'pass away,' though believers differ over when 'the perfect' comes). Second, this does not mean God no longer works miracles: he remains free to heal and act wonderfully in answer to prayer, and often does. What ceased is the apostolic sign-gift as a standing credential of new revelation — not God's power or nearness. (Bible-loving Christians differ here; this is the historic cessationist reading these notes follow.)

'Solomon's Portico' was a long, covered colonnade — a roofed walkway of great columns — along the east side of the temple's outer court. Tradition linked it to Solomon, though it belonged to Herod's temple. It was a well-known public teaching place: Jesus had walked there (John 10:23), and Peter had preached there after healing the lame man (Acts 3:11). That the believers met there 'all together' is striking — not huddled in hiding but gathered openly in the most public religious space in Jerusalem, in the temple's very shadow. The holy, fearless church stood out in plain sight.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'None of the rest dared join them' — and 'the rest' is a fair puzzle: it can hardly mean true believers (they had already gladly joined), yet plain unbelievers would not be 'joining' the church anyway. The word 'join' (kollasthai) means to glue oneself closely — so 'the rest' are best understood as the fringe: the half-hearted, the curious, the would-be hangers-on who in a less sobered moment might have attached themselves to so admired and powerful a movement for the prestige or the perks. After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared. The community's fearful holiness (vv. 5, 11) had raised the cost of insincere belonging to terrifying clarity: you do not glue yourself to this people for mixed motives. So this verse and the next are two sides of one coin — v. 13: the nominal and false no longer dared press in; v. 14: 'yet more than ever believers were added.' The fear screened out the pretenders while the Spirit kept adding the genuine — the church purified and multiplied at once. (Commentators differ on 'the rest'; but this reading, straight out of the Ananias episode, is the most natural.)

'But the people held them in high esteem' — worth pausing over, because the church's public welcome runs hot and cold through Acts: esteemed here, arrested a few verses on (5:17–18), and soon Stephen stoned amid great persecution (chs. 7–8). Is there a pattern? Several, though no rigid formula. First, the fault line often runs between the common people and the authorities: crowds admired the apostles while threatened rulers persecuted them — and the people's esteem actually shielded them, for the officers dared use no force, 'afraid of being stoned by the people' (5:26). Early persecution is mostly top-down. Second, public favour is real but fickle — the same city can cheer and then turn, as 'Hosanna' became 'Crucify.' Third, both favour and hostility serve God's purposes and come from his hand: he grants seasons of favour to open doors (2:47) and permits persecution to scatter the seed and spread the word (8:1–4). So the believer should be neither intoxicated by esteem nor crushed by opposition. Scripture holds both: 'when a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him' (Prov. 16:7), yet 'all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted' (2 Tim. 3:12). Esteem is a gift, received humbly and spent for Christ; persecution is the long-run lot of faithful witness (John 15:20). Both, in God's hands, advance the same kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the sentence that ought to surprise us and rarely does. Two people have dropped dead on the floor of the meeting. The city has heard about it. Nobody outside dares attach himself to this movement casually any more (v. 13). And the result is not decline. More than ever believers were added to the Lord. The comparative is deliberate: more than before the deaths, not fewer.

Everything in modern instinct says that is the wrong way round. We assume a church grows by lowering the temperature — by being easier to belong to, less demanding, less strange, more like the surrounding culture with a religious accent. Luke reports the opposite happening. When it became unmistakably clear that the God in that room was real and was not to be handled carelessly, the pretenders stopped coming and everyone else started. The two movements in verses 13 and 14 are one movement: the fear screened out the casual and the Spirit kept adding the genuine. A church can be crowded and thin at the same time, and there is a kind of clarity that costs a congregation its hangers-on and gains it a city.

That is not, however, a licence for severity, and the distinction matters because it has been abused. The fear in Acts 5 came from something God did, not from something the leadership did. Peter did not strike anyone, threaten anyone, or run a campaign of discipline; he asked two honest questions and God did the rest. A church where people are frightened of the elders, watch their words in the foyer, and cannot admit a struggle without consequences has not reproduced this chapter. It has produced the very thing this chapter killed: a community where everyone performs. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

Then the phrase worth dwelling on: they were added to the Lord. Not to the church, not to the movement, not to a register. Luke could have written either and wrote neither. What happens when a person is converted is that he is joined to a Person, and membership among the people follows because they belong to him too. Anyone who has ever wondered whether he is in because he signed something, attends something, or is liked by someone has the answer here: the attachment that counts was made to the Lord himself, and it will therefore outlast every congregation any of us ever belongs to.

And Luke counts the women. Multitudes of both men and women — he says it as a matter of course, in a world where a crowd was ordinarily numbered by its men. At Pentecost Peter had stood up and read out Joel's promise that God would pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, on male and female servants alike (2:17–18). A few weeks later Luke writes the growth figures, and the promise is simply showing in the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healing ministry has reached a scale that draws the entire Jerusalem region and beyond. 'That at least his shadow might fall' — this is popular faith expressing itself in folk terms; Luke does not say the shadow healed anyone, but the faith that drove people to lay the sick in Peter's path was honored by God.
