'They were all healed' — Luke's summaries of healing are consistently comprehensive. The kingdom has arrived; creation is being restored; the preview of the new creation is visible in the streets of Jerusalem.

'Those afflicted with unclean spirits' raises the hard subject of the demonic, and here we should say only what Scripture actually tells us. 'Unclean spirits' are real, personal, evil spirit-beings — what the Gospels equally call 'demons,' using the two terms interchangeably (e.g. Mark 5:2, 12–15; 7:25–26). They are not mere symbols, nor simply an ancient label for illness; the New Testament treats them as intelligent beings with will and speech, part of the kingdom of Satan (Matt. 12:24–26) and commonly understood as fallen angels (Rev. 12:9; 2 Pet. 2:4). 'Unclean' marks their nature: they are defiling, the very opposite of the holiness of God. They can oppress and torment, and at times control a person, with effects both physical (muteness, convulsions, even unnatural strength — Matt. 9:32–33; Mark 5:3–4; 9:18) and inward (the torment of mind and soul, Mark 5:5). Note, though, that Scripture does not blame every sickness on demons: it deliberately lists 'the sick' and 'those afflicted with unclean spirits' as two distinct groups (here, and Mark 1:32–34) — so we are neither to deny the demonic nor to see a demon behind every illness.

What Scripture stresses above all is their relation to Christ. The unclean spirits recognize him and tremble (Mark 1:24; James 2:19), are utterly subject to his authority and to his name on the lips of his servants (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18), and flee before the advancing kingdom: 'if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28). At the cross he 'disarmed the rulers and authorities... triumphing over them' (Col. 2:15). So when Luke writes that here 'they were all healed,' he is displaying the kingdom's triumph: where Christ's gospel advances, the unclean spirits retreat. As for the rest — how exactly a spirit afflicts, the line between oppression and possession, why some and not others — Scripture is reticent, and we will not pretend to know more than it tells us. It gives us enough to take the reality seriously, never to fear it, and to look only to the Conqueror: 'he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world' (1 John 4:4).

On the purpose of such healings and exorcisms as 'signs and wonders' — given to authenticate the apostolic message rather than as ends in themselves, and the question of whether these sign-gifts continue today — see the commentary on v. 12.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The high priest and the Sadducean party, filled with jealousy, arrest the apostles a second time and put them in the public prison — a deliberate humiliation. During the night an angel opens the doors and sends them back to the one place they must not go: stand in the temple and speak all the words of this Life. They are there at daybreak. Meanwhile the council convenes in full solemn session, sends for prisoners who are no longer there, and receives a report that is a small masterpiece of bewilderment: the prison securely locked, the guards at their posts, and nobody inside. The men receiving that report are the party which holds that there is no resurrection, no angel and no spirit; they are handed a sealed and empty room and never once ask how.

The second hearing produces the sharpest exchange in Acts so far. The high priest will not say the name of Jesus, complaining only that these men intend to bring this man's blood upon them — the bloodguilt they had once called down on themselves. Peter's answer is the church's permanent one: we must obey God rather than men, followed at once by the gospel itself, preached to the court that has him in custody. God raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree; God has exalted him as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance and forgiveness; and there are two witnesses to it, the apostles and the Holy Spirit.

The council is enraged and wants to kill them. What saves them is not an angel this time but an old Pharisee whose opinion the room cannot dismiss. Gamaliel counsels delay from two failed movements, warns that they might even be found opposing God, and is taken at his word only far enough to reduce the sentence: the apostles are flogged, charged again to be silent, and released. And the chapter closes on the answer to that charge. They left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the Name, and every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God Rather Than Men

Gamaliel's advice — if it is of man it will fail, if it is of God you cannot overthrow it — is often praised as tolerance. It is not Christian reasoning. It is pragmatic patience that never distinguishes truth from falsehood, only durable movements from short-lived ones, and it allows a man to avoid the one question in the room: did God raise Jesus? He is a providential restraint, not a theological authority. The apostles rest their case on something else entirely. Their principle is not defiance but a hierarchy of obedience: the state's authority is real and derived, and a delegated authority that forbids what God commands has run out of warrant at that point and no further. The same New Testament that records these words commands submission to governing authorities under Nero (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17). And the apostles supply the test that keeps the principle honest — they did not resist arrest, did not raise the crowd that was ready to riot for them, and did not flee. They took the flogging. Biblical civil disobedience always carries the penalty; it never comes with an escape clause.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the Name — led by the man who, seven weeks earlier, had denied that he knew Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire. What changed was not his temperament.

Now: Suffering for the Name is not masochism and joy in it is not a duty to be manufactured in advance; it was given to those men on the way out of the building. Two things this passage is not: it is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person, since the suffering in view is dishonour incurred for Christ; and it is not a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes. The question is always whether God is being forbidden what he commands — and whether one is prepared to bear the cost of saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The party of the Sadducees' — a word on who they were, since they now become the apostles' chief persecutors. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem: the wealthy, ruling, temple-controlling families, and the high priest himself was their head (hence 'the high priest... and all who were with him, that is, the party of the Sadducees'). The temple and its vast establishment were theirs; they dominated the priestly side of the Sanhedrin and, as the men who profited from the status quo, cooperated closely with Rome to keep their power. Theologically they accepted only the written Law of Moses (the first five books) as binding, rejected the oral traditions the Pharisees prized, and — crucially here — denied the resurrection of the dead, along with angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). Their name most likely derives from Zadok, Solomon's high priest (1 Kings 2:35; cf. the 'sons of Zadok,' Ezek. 44:15), marking them as the party of the old priestly line; they had emerged as a distinct group in the two centuries before Christ (the precise origins are not certain). All of which explains the heat of their reaction: the apostles were filling Jerusalem with the message of a risen Jesus — the very doctrine of resurrection the Sadducees denied (cf. Acts 4:1–2) — and were drawing the people's allegiance away from the temple establishment. The gospel struck at both their theology and their power.

'Filled with jealousy' — the motivation for the second arrest is stated explicitly. The apostles' growing influence and public esteem have provoked the envy of the religious establishment. The Sadducees who deny resurrection are watching a community built entirely on resurrection faith grow exponentially under their noses. The arrest is a response to success — every closure the authorities attempt is prompted by the gospel's advance. The world's opposition to the gospel is always, at root, a form of jealousy: the kingdom of God wins the allegiance that human institutions cannot command.

Two details in the arrest are worth having. The word for their jealousy (zelos) is not petty envy but hot zeal — the burning of men who believe something precious is being taken from them, which is exactly what a religious establishment feels when the people begin listening to somebody else. And they put the apostles in the public prison, the common lock-up, not a holding room in the temple. That was a choice. It was meant to be seen, and to be degrading: the men Jerusalem had begun to admire, walked through the streets and put in with the ordinary criminals.

Underneath it all sits the fact that governs this entire chapter. The men now running the case against the resurrection are the party that has staked its theology on there being no such thing. This is the third time the council has been confronted with the claim that Jesus of Nazareth is alive — and in all three encounters, from the guards' report at the tomb to this morning's empty cell, not one member of it is recorded as asking the only question that matters: is it true? They investigate the preachers. They never investigate the claim. It is possible to hold the highest office in the religion of the living God and to have no interest whatever in whether he has done something.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke spends one clause on the miracle. An angel of the Lord opened the doors and brought them out. No description of the angel, no reaction from the apostles, no word about the guards, no drama at all. The escape is not the story. What the angel says next is the story, and it is one of the most bracing sentences in the book: go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.

Consider what is not said. Not go home. Not lie low until this passes. Not leave Jerusalem, which would have been the obvious counsel and which no reasonable adviser would have withheld. They are told to go straight back to the building owned and policed by the men who had just locked them up, at the busiest hour of the morning, and do precisely the thing they were arrested for doing. Heaven broke into a prison in order to put men back in the place of maximum danger. The rescue was not a rescue from anything; it was a transfer to the front.

And the phrase the angel uses for the message is unusual enough to be worth holding: all the words of this Life. Not the words about this life, and not the message of eternal life in the abstract. This Life — the thing standing in front of everybody, the life that came out of a sealed tomb and is now visibly loose in Jerusalem, healing people in the street and putting courage into fishermen. Speak all of it, the angel says. All the words. Not the parts the council will tolerate.

But a prison that opens raises a question that has to be met honestly, because it is the question a suffering reader will bring, and this book itself refuses to duck it. Why does God open this door and not others? Turn forward seven chapters and Luke tells you about another night, another angel, another set of chains falling off Peter — and in the same paragraph, James the brother of John put to death with the sword, and no angel came (12:1–11). One apostle walks out past the guards; the other is buried. Luke sets them side by side without a word of explanation, and he did not have to. He could easily have left the beheading out. Later in the same book Paul will sit in custody for two full years while a governor waits for a bribe (24:26–27), and no angel comes for him either, and some of the most useful letters ever written come out of that silence.

So this passage must never be turned into a promise that the door opens for the faithful. The doors that stayed shut in this very book were shut on better men than most of us, and it was never a question of whether they had believed hard enough. What Acts actually teaches is narrower and steadier: God opens what he needs opened for the gospel to go where he intends it to go, and he is under no obligation to explain his selection to anyone. James's death scattered nothing and stopped nothing. Paul's two wasted years produced letters the church has never been without.

Which gives an ordinary Christian a better question than 'why has my door not opened.' Look at what the angel actually did with these men once they were out. Every deliverance in Acts is for the mission, never for the comfort of the delivered — and this one lasted about six hours before the same men were arrested again and flogged before sundown. Anyone who has been brought out of something, a diagnosis or a debt or a marriage that nearly ended, has a plainer thing to ask than why it happened to him and not to someone else. He can ask what he has been let out for. In this chapter the answer came with the door.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simple and stunning: they heard, they went, they taught. By daybreak they are back in the temple — the very building controlled by the men who imprisoned them — teaching exactly what they were imprisoned for teaching. No deliberation, no calculation of risk, no consultation about whether to obey the angel. The obedience is immediate and complete. This is the pattern of apostolic ministry throughout Acts: when God opens a door (literally or figuratively), the missionaries walk through it without hesitation.

Meanwhile the other half of the verse shows the establishment swinging into action: 'the high priest... called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.' The 'council' is the Sanhedrin (synedrion), the supreme ruling court of the Jewish nation — seventy members presided over by the high priest (seventy-one in all), drawn from the chief priests (Sadducees), the elders (the lay aristocracy and heads of leading families), and the scribes (the legal experts, largely Pharisees). It was the highest religious and judicial body in Israel, meeting in the temple precincts, with authority over Jewish law — though under Rome a death sentence still needed the governor's ratification (cf. John 18:31). 'All the senate of the people of Israel' (gerousia, the council of elders) is Luke piling term upon term to stress that they convened the entire official body in its most solemn, formal session — a term with deep roots, for a 'senate of elders' had governed the nation since the days of the Maccabees and before, and grew into the Sanhedrin. And here is the quiet irony Luke means us to feel: the full might of the establishment is ponderously assembled, and officers are sent to fetch prisoners — who are no longer there. The grandest court in Israel grinds into motion against men God has already set free and who are, at that very hour, teaching in the temple.

One more word about the timing. Luke says they entered the temple at daybreak — at first light, the earliest hour the gates opened. They had been let out in the middle of the night and they went straight there and waited for the doors. There is no interval in the sentence for a discussion about whether the angel had really meant it, or whether it might be wiser to let a day pass. The obedience did not consult anything. A great deal of what passes for seeking God's will is the search for a delay he has not granted, and these men, who had every reason to want one, did not take it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, and they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers' report is a small masterpiece and Luke lets it stand without a word of comment. Everything is exactly as it should be. The prison securely locked. The guards at their posts, awake, doing their job, having seen nothing. And when the door is opened, nobody inside. Every element of the system worked perfectly and the men are gone. There is no human account of it available to anybody in the room, and the officers do not attempt one; they simply describe what they found and let their superiors make of it what they can.

Notice how God did it, because the manner is a signature. The doors were not blown off their hinges. The guards were not struck down, or blinded, or thrown into a sleep they would have to explain. Nothing was broken and nobody was hurt. The doors were opened and then closed again behind eleven men walking out into the dark. The whole miracle is tidy, and it is the tidiness that is unnerving: this is not power straining against resistance, it is power to which locked doors are not an obstacle worth damaging.

And now stand back and look at the shape of what these particular men are being asked to explain. A sealed place. Guards posted. An occupant who was certainly there last night. And in the morning, everything secure and the place empty, with nothing but an account nobody can produce. Jerusalem had heard that story once already, seven weeks before, about a tomb, and this council had done its best to keep the lid on it. Now the same shape has turned up in their own jail.

Who is receiving the report makes it sharper still. Luke has just told us that the men driving this arrest are the party of the Sadducees (v. 17), and the Sadducees are on record in this book as the people who say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (23:8). An angel has just emptied their prison. They are standing in a room holding a report of an empty cell, delivered by honest witnesses, about men who cannot be accounted for — and the only conclusion available is the one their theology has ruled out in advance. They will spend the rest of the chapter trying to manage the consequences of a fact they have decided cannot happen.

That is worth carrying out of the passage, because it is a very modern condition. It is entirely possible to have all the evidence in hand, in order, from reliable sources, and to be unable to reach the obvious conclusion — not because the evidence is weak but because the conclusion has already been excluded. The officers reported accurately. Nobody disputed the facts. And the council's next move was not to ask how it had happened; it was to send for the men and tell them to stop talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The perplexity of the authorities is genuine — they cannot explain the empty prison, and they have no strategy for what it means. 'Wondering what this would come to' — they sense that events are moving in a direction they cannot control. The interruption of someone's arrival with news is almost farcical: the men you imprisoned are back in the temple teaching. The cycle of arrest and proclamation is already completing its second revolution. The word that the authorities cannot silence is being proclaimed in the building they control.

A brief word on the two named here. The 'captain of the temple' (stratēgos; Hebrew sagan) was the chief officer of the temple, second in rank only to the high priest himself — a senior priest who commanded the Levitical temple guard, kept order in the precincts, held the power of arrest (it was he who helped seize Jesus, Luke 22:4, 52, and the apostles, Acts 4:1), and was often the high priest's deputy and next in line. The 'chief priests' (archiereis) were the priestly aristocracy at the top of the temple hierarchy: the high priest, former high priests who kept the title and influence, and the heads of the leading priestly families — a small, mostly Sadducean elite who controlled the temple administration and were prominent in the Sanhedrin. In short, this is the temple's entire ruling establishment — its head of security and its senior clergy — standing helpless and 'greatly perplexed' before an empty cell.

Luke's word for their state (diaporeo) means to be at a complete loss, thrown back on nothing — not merely puzzled but out of options for an explanation. And what they are said to be doing with the perplexity is telling: wondering what this would come to. They are not asking what has happened; they are asking where it ends. Men who have felt the ground shift under an institution know that particular anxiety, and it is a more honest reaction than anything they will say for the rest of the day.

Then comes one of the finest anticlimaxes in Scripture. Into that silence, someone arrives, and Luke gives us the man's opening word: Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people. Not fled. Not hiding. Not across the border. Standing, in the establishment's own building, doing the thing at which they were interrupted, while the establishment holds an emergency session about where they might have gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The captain of the temple goes to fetch them himself, and Luke records the manner in four words that carry the whole chapter: but not by force. The head of temple security, with his officers, in his own precinct, arresting men he has the legal right to arrest, and he does it carefully, apologetically, almost politely — because he is frightened of the crowd. The men who hold every instrument of power in Jerusalem cannot use any of it, and the reason is given plainly: they were afraid of being stoned by the people.

Now put that beside what Luke has been telling us for the last fifteen verses, because he has built this chapter around one word. Great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5). Great fear came upon the whole church (v. 11). And now fear again — on the other side of the room, in the other party, with a different object. Both groups in this chapter are afraid. The church is afraid of God. The council is afraid of the public. Nobody in the Sanhedrin appears to be afraid of God at all, and that is exactly why they are afraid of everybody else.

It is a rule with almost no exceptions. A man who genuinely fears God has one thing to be afraid of and is therefore free of nearly everything; a man who does not ends up managing a long and growing list. The council cannot act on its convictions, cannot speak its mind, cannot follow its own legal judgement, because it has to keep watching the temple courts to see how it is playing. Every decision they take from here to the end of the chapter is shaped by a crowd they despise. That is the price of having replaced conscience with reputation, and it is not paid only by first-century aristocrats. Anyone who has ever softened a conviction because of what a room would think has felt the same rope round the same neck.

The contrast with the men being fetched could hardly be sharper. The apostles have just been let out of that prison by an angel, are standing in a temple full of people who admire them, and have every opportunity to refuse, to slip away in the crowd, or to let the crowd do what the officers plainly fear it would do. They do none of it. They walk back with the officers and stand in front of the council. The one group in Jerusalem with real reason to be afraid is the one group behaving as though there were nothing to fear.

And there is a quiet lesson in the fact that the crowd's goodwill is what is protecting them at this moment. It is a real protection and God is plainly using it. It is also a protection with a short shelf life, and none of these men is leaning on it. Within two chapters the mood of this same city will have turned far enough for Stephen to be stoned by it. Public favour is a gift to be received and spent, never a foundation to build on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest's complaint is an inadvertent testimony: 'you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching.' The very thing they were trying to prevent has happened on a city-wide scale. 'You intend to bring this man's blood upon us' — the council's bad conscience about the crucifixion surfaces. They know what they did; they fear the crowd's reaction; and they cannot silence the ones who keep announcing it. 'This man's blood' — they will not speak the name. The refusal to name Jesus is the first of many failed attempts to suppress him by silence.

'To bring this man's blood upon us' uses an old Hebrew idiom for bloodguilt — to hold someone responsible for a death, to lay the guilt of it at his door (Lev. 20:9; Josh. 2:19; 2 Sam. 1:16; Ezek. 33:4). The council fears the apostles are publicly fastening on them the charge of having murdered Jesus — and they are quite right to fear it, for that is exactly what the apostles have been doing: 'you crucified and killed' him, 'whom you killed by hanging him on a tree' (Acts 2:23, 36; 3:15; 5:30). The irony is bitter: at Jesus' trial this same leadership had stirred the crowd to cry, 'His blood be on us and on our children!' (Matt. 27:25) — they once called the bloodguilt down on themselves; now they are terrified of being held to it. But notice where their fear is aimed — not at their guilt, but at the men who name it. They want to silence the accusation rather than be cleansed of the blood, and that is their tragedy. For there was a way to be rid of this man's blood, and it was not to muzzle the preachers but to be washed in the very blood they had shed. The blood that lay 'upon them' as guilt was being held out to them as atonement: 'repent... for the forgiveness of your sins' (Acts 2:36–38). The accusation and the cure were one and the same blood.

One word in the complaint deserves to be traced, because Luke has been laying a thread through this whole chapter and it comes to the surface here. The high priest says the apostles have filled Jerusalem with their teaching. It is the third filling in twenty-eight verses. Satan filled Ananias's heart to lie (v. 3). The high priest and his party were filled with jealousy (v. 17). And now the city itself is filled with the message they were forbidden to speak. Luke is showing what happens when the Spirit fills a church: everything in the chapter that sets itself against him is also full of something, and none of it can hold ground. A heart full of the adversary lasted a morning. A council full of envy could reach no further than a whip. The teaching filled a capital city and has not stopped.

And there is one more unintended admission in the sentence. We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem. Every word of that is a report of the council's own failure, delivered in the tone of an accusation. They are complaining, under oath, in open session, that the gospel is unstoppable. The prosecution has just entered the defence's best evidence into the record.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have been arrested twice, held overnight, released by an angel, re-arrested before an assembled Sanhedrin, and formally charged with breaking a court order. And Peter's reply is a single sentence with no preamble and no apology in it: we must obey God rather than men. The verb is the strong one — it is necessary, it is binding, there is no other course open to us. He is not claiming a right. He is describing an obligation he has no power to set aside.

This is the second time these men have said it to this court. The first was two chapters ago, softer, framed as a question they invited the council to answer for itself: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge (4:19). The council has now had its answer and repeated its order, and so the question becomes a statement. That is worth noticing about Christian conscience — it does not usually start by shouting. It asks first, and only hardens when the asking has been refused.

But because this sentence is quoted so often, and by people in very different situations, it needs its frame put back around it, or it becomes a slogan for whatever a believer happens to want to defy. The New Testament's ordinary teaching about government is not resistance but submission, and it is stated in the strongest terms by men living under an empire that would shortly execute both of them. Be subject to the governing authorities, Paul writes, for there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1) — written to Christians in Nero's capital city. Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, writes Peter, honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:13–17) — written by the man speaking these very words, to churches about to feel what that emperor could do. Neither of them regarded obedience to the state as a concession wrung out of them. They regarded it as obedience to God.

So how do the two fit? By recognising that the authority of a government is real and derived. It is genuine authority, and it is held on delegation. A magistrate has his warrant from God, which is why a Christian obeys him in the ordinary run of things without needing to agree with him. But a delegated authority that commands what the one who delegated it forbids has, at that precise point, run out of warrant — and only at that point. Scripture supplies the pattern before Acts ever does: midwives who would not kill the boys and lied to Pharaoh about it (Exodus 1:17), three men who would not bow to a statue and said so without knowing whether they would be spared (Daniel 3:16–18), an old official who kept his windows open toward Jerusalem when praying had been made a capital offence (Daniel 6:10).

Which yields a test an ordinary Christian can actually apply, and it is narrower than most people who quote this verse would like. The question is not whether a law is unwise, unfair, expensive, or offensive to me. The question is whether I am being commanded to do what God forbids, or forbidden to do what God commands. The apostles are in the second case: God had told them, that very morning and through an angel, to go and speak (v. 20). A tax I resent, a policy I judge foolish, a regulation that inconveniences my church — none of these is Acts 5, and dressing them in this verse cheapens the verse for the day it is genuinely needed.

And there is a second half of the test, which is the half almost always dropped. Look at what these men do not do. They do not resist arrest, though an angel had just demonstrated that the doors were no obstacle. They do not summon the crowd, though Luke has just told us the officers were afraid of exactly that and it would have worked. They do not flee the city. They walk in, state their position, take a flogging for it, and go back to work. Biblical civil disobedience always comes with a willingness to bear the penalty; it never comes with an escape clause. Anyone appealing to this verse who is unwilling to pay the fine, take the sentence, or lose the position is appealing to something other than what Peter is doing here.

Then, having refused the court's authority, Peter immediately exercises it. He does not merely defend the preaching; he preaches, on the spot, to the men who have him in custody. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. Every phrase is chosen. The God of our fathers claims continuity — this is not a new religion appearing beside Israel's but the God of Abraham keeping his word, and it is the council, not the apostles, who have broken step. Whom you killed is said to their faces, in their own chamber, by a man who has no legal standing whatsoever.

And hanging him on a tree is the most deliberate phrase of all. Peter could have said crucified; he has said it before. Instead he reaches for the language of Deuteronomy, where a man hung on a tree is cursed by God, an object of horror to be taken down before nightfall so the land is not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:23). He picks the one description of the cross most offensive to every man listening, and he picks it because it is the truth about what happened there. The curse was real. It fell. It simply was not his. He was hung on that tree under a curse he had not earned, in the place of people who had earned it and could not carry it, and the God of their fathers raised him to prove the account was settled. There is no gospel available that does not go through that sentence, and Peter puts it in front of his judges within a minute of being told to shut up.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Leader and Savior' (archēgon kai sōtēra) — the crucified one is now the Leader who blazed the trail through death to resurrection and the Savior who offers repentance and forgiveness. 'To give repentance to Israel' — repentance itself is God's gift, not human achievement; the same God who commands it supplies it through the exalted Jesus. Two witnesses testify to these things: the apostles (human eyewitnesses of the resurrection) and the Holy Spirit (divine confirmation given to those who obey). The council cannot refute either witness.

In what way is the Holy Spirit a 'witness'? Jesus had promised exactly this pairing: 'the Spirit of truth... will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness' (John 15:26–27) — two witnesses, as the Law required (Deut. 19:15). The Spirit testifies in several joined ways. First by his very outpouring, since the fact that God has poured out the Spirit is itself proof that the crucified Jesus is risen and enthroned, for only the exalted Christ could send him — 'having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves see and hear' (Acts 2:33). The Spirit's presence in the church is living evidence of the resurrection the apostles proclaim. He testifies, too, by empowering the witnesses themselves, emboldening them and speaking through them (Acts 1:8; 4:8, 31). He testifies outwardly, in the signs and wonders and the transformed, multiplying church — God bearing witness 'by gifts of the Holy Spirit' (Heb. 2:4). And he testifies inwardly, pressing the truth home on the conscience, convicting the world of sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11) and confirming the gospel within the believer (Rom. 8:16). So the council faces not merely the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself: a witness they can imprison no more than they could keep the prison shut.

Two things in the first half of Peter's sentence should not be hurried past. Leader renders archegos, a word with no tidy English equivalent: it carries the sense of the one who goes first and opens the way — a pioneer who cuts the track others will walk, a founder in whom a whole people begins. Peter is saying that Jesus did not merely arrange a rescue from a safe distance. He went through death himself, first, and came out the other side, and the road exists because he made it. Nobody who follows him into that country will be going anywhere he has not already been.

And then, quietly, the phrase that ought to stop anybody who has ever tried and failed to repent: God exalted him to give repentance. Repentance is here a thing handed over, not a thing achieved. That cuts against the way most people instinctively hear the command — as though God stands at a distance requiring a change of heart that we must manufacture before he will look at us. Peter says the exalted Christ dispenses it. Anyone who has genuinely wanted to be sorry for something and found that he could only regret the consequences knows the difference between working up remorse and being given a new mind about a thing. The first cannot be done to order. The second is a gift, and the place to go for it is the one who was exalted to hand it out.

One clause here needs a guard, because it has been misused: the Spirit is given to those who obey him. Read carelessly that turns the Spirit into a wage. But the obedience Peter has in mind is not a record of performance; it is the same word he used of himself two verses earlier, when he said we must obey God rather than men — and what he meant there was believing God's word about his Son and acting on it. That is the obedience the New Testament calls the obedience of faith. The Spirit is not the prize for a life already put right. He is the one who puts it right, and he comes to people whose response to the message about Jesus has been surrender rather than management.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council's response to the apostolic declaration is rage — not refutation, not deliberation, but the visceral fury of those whose authority has been publicly and repeatedly defied. They 'wanted to kill them' — the same impulse that led to the crucifixion is now directed at his witnesses. But God's providential care for his messengers operates through an unlikely instrument: Gamaliel, the most respected Pharisee of his generation (Paul's own teacher, 22:3), whose caution and authority are sufficient to pause the council's murderous intent.

Beyond the New Testament, Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about Gamaliel — though it is best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder (Gamaliel I), one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by Jewish tradition, a descendant (commonly, the grandson) of the famed Hillel and a leader of Hillel's school; he is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the exalted title 'Rabban' ('our master'), a rank above 'Rabbi.' The Mishnah pays him a striking tribute: 'When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and piety died' (Sotah 9:15). Tradition also credits him with several legal rulings (takkanot) made for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce (Mishnah Gittin 4). And, as Luke notes elsewhere, the young Saul of Tarsus — the future apostle Paul — was trained 'at the feet of Gamaliel' (Acts 22:3). (A much later Christian legend claimed Gamaliel secretly became a believer and that his remains were found in AD 415; but this has no historical foundation and should be set aside.)

Luke's word for the council's rage repays a moment. They were, literally, sawn through — cut in two by what they had heard. And that is worth setting beside the only other place in Acts where a crowd hears an apostolic sermon and is described as being cut. On the day of Pentecost the people were cut to the heart and said, brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here the same message, delivered by the same man, about the same risen Christ, cuts men in exactly the same place and produces a decision to kill him. Stephen will meet the identical reaction from this identical body a chapter later, and it will finish the way it wanted to finish here (7:54).

That is the sober truth about preaching Christ, and it is a comfort as well as a warning. The gospel is never neutral and it very rarely leaves people where it found them; it either breaks a man open or hardens him, and the wound feels much the same from the inside at first. Three thousand went one way in chapter 2. This council went the other. Nothing in the message had changed.

And into that room, at the moment murder is being openly proposed by the supreme court of Israel, God sends a Pharisee. Not an angel this time, not an earthquake, not a miracle of any kind. A respected old teacher stands up and asks for the room to be cleared, and eleven men live. Providence does not always arrive with the doors opening of their own accord; sometimes it arrives as the one person present whose opinion the others cannot afford to dismiss.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, followed him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel opens with a warning, and it is worth registering how serious it is. Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. He is addressing the supreme court of his nation, in session, which has just openly proposed killing eleven prisoners without a trial, and he tells them to be careful. He is the only man in the chamber who says anything of the kind.

His argument is drawn entirely from recent memory. Judea in living recollection had produced a run of men who gathered a following, claimed to be somebody, and came to nothing when they were killed. Gamaliel names one, and will name a second, and his reasoning is simple: movements of that kind collapse when their leader dies, so let time do the work and keep the council's hands clean. (The two names he cites carry a long-standing historical objection to Luke's accuracy; it is answered on vv. 37-38.)

As practical advice it is shrewd, and God used it, and eleven men went home alive because of it. As a way of settling what is true it is worthless, and it is worth being clear about why, because the same reasoning is offered constantly today in a religious voice. Durability is not a test of truth. Plenty of false things last for centuries; Gamaliel was making his case inside a temple that had stood a long time and was forty years from being rubble. Plenty of true things are crushed early and stay crushed for a generation. Applied consistently, his rule would have condemned nearly every prophet Israel ever had, all of whom were dismissed, imprisoned or killed and none of whom looked durable at the time.

The deeper problem is that Gamaliel's rule allows a man to avoid the only question in the room. The apostles had not asked the council to predict their movement's future. They had made a factual claim: God raised Jesus from the dead, and we saw him. That claim can be investigated. It has witnesses, a location, a date, and an empty tomb whose emptiness nobody in that chamber disputed. Gamaliel proposes instead that they wait and observe the outcome — which is a decision not to look.

That posture is extremely common and it is always presented as open-mindedness. If Christianity is real it will survive without my verdict; if it is not, my verdict will not have mattered. It sounds humble and it is in fact the one position that cannot be held. A man deciding whether Jesus rose from the dead is not an observer of the case; he is a party to it. Waiting to see how it turns out is itself an answer, and it is the answer given by everyone who has ever intended to look into it properly later. Gamaliel had the evidence, the intelligence, and the standing to settle it, and he chose the one course that required nothing of him. So far as Scripture records, he died having chosen it.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas the Galilean's revolt at the time of Quirinius's census (AD 6) was better known and more politically charged than Theudas's movement — the mention of it would have resonated deeply with the council. Gamaliel's principle ('if it is of man, it will fail') is the kind of wisdom that sounds profound but avoids the actual question: is it of God? His counsel is a deferral, not a judgment. But it serves God's purpose: the apostles are not killed, the mission continues, and Gamaliel himself is perhaps set wondering whether this movement is different from the ones he named.

These two names carry a well-known objection, and since Luke's standing as a historian matters to this whole book it should be met. Josephus describes a Theudas who led a revolt under the procurator Fadus, and dates it to about AD 44 — a decade or more after Gamaliel is speaking here. Worse, Gamaliel places Judas the Galilean, whose rising came at the census of AD 6, after Theudas. On the face of it Luke has the order backwards and the date impossible, and this is regularly produced as proof that he invented the speech.

Two things need saying. The first is that Theudas was a common name in a country that was full of failed insurgents. Josephus himself says that after Herod the Great died in 4 BC there were countless disturbances in Judea, and he names several leaders who gathered a following and were cut down. Gamaliel's Theudas had about four hundred men; the one Josephus dates to the forties drew a great crowd to the Jordan. There is no difficulty in supposing two men of the same name, forty years apart, in a generation that produced rebels by the dozen.

The second is worth weighing before conceding anything. The objection assumes that where Luke and Josephus differ, Josephus is the standard and Luke the suspect. Josephus is a valuable historian and a demonstrably careless one in places, and that assumption has not aged well. Luke was long said to have blundered over the titles of local officials — the politarchs of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the first man of Malta — and inscription after inscription has since shown him exactly right, in details a forger would have had no way to know. A writer with that record has earned the benefit of the doubt about a rebel's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel's last sentence is the sharpest thing said in the chamber all day, and he almost certainly did not know how sharp it was. You might even be found opposing God. The word he uses (theomachoi, God-fighters) appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it did not come out of the synagogue; it belonged to the world of Greek tragedy, where the man who sets himself against heaven is destroyed by the attempt, usually while believing he is defending something. Gamaliel raises it as a remote hazard, a possibility worth insuring against. It is the actual position of every man he is speaking to.

And that is the exquisite thing about the sentence. He describes the council's situation with perfect accuracy while presenting it as a hypothesis. They are not at risk of opposing God; they have arrested his messengers twice, ignored an empty prison reported by their own officers, and just now discussed murdering eleven men for saying that God raised Jesus. The wisest man in the room got nearer to the truth than anyone else present and still treated it as a remote contingency. It is possible to be right about God in the conditional and wrong about him in the indicative.

Then Luke writes five flat words: so they took his advice. And the next verse tells you exactly what taking it amounted to. They did not kill the apostles; they had them stripped and flogged and repeated the order to be silent. So this is what a court does when it has been warned that it may be fighting God: it reduces the sentence and carries on. Gamaliel's own argument, taken seriously for five minutes, demanded an investigation, because a body told there is a real possibility it is at war with the Almighty cannot rationally respond by doing nothing and waiting. Nobody proposes finding out. They amend the punishment and move to the next item.

There is a further quiet irony that Luke may well intend his reader to catch later. Three chapters from here a young man is standing at a stoning, holding the coats, approving; and he tells us himself that he was brought up in this city at the feet of this same Gamaliel (22:3). Saul of Tarsus had this exact warning from his own teacher, and went out and did the very thing it warned against, until a voice on a road asked him why he was persecuting me. Gamaliel's word turned out to be a prophecy about his best student.

But the sentence to carry away from this scene is not about Gamaliel at all. Eleven men who could not defend themselves, in the hands of a court that wanted them dead, were delivered by an argument they did not make, from a man who was not on their side, for reasons that were not the right ones. The church's survival that morning did not depend on its case being heard, its friends being influential, or its enemies being reasonable. It never has. What Gamaliel offered as a warning against a possibility, the apostles could have offered as a statement of fact: nothing that is of God will be overthrown, and the men holding the whip have never once been told what the outcome would be.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council cannot kill the apostles (Gamaliel's counsel has prevented it) but they can punish them — and they do: forty lashes less one (the standard Jewish punishment for contempt of authority). The charge is repeated: 'not to speak in the name of Jesus.' The beating is meant to break the boldness; the charge is meant to silence the proclamation. Neither will succeed. The apostles emerge from the flogging not broken but unbowed, not silent but more vocal. Suffering for the name does not diminish their willingness to speak it.

A brief word for the everyday reader on what 'speaking in the name of Jesus' means. In the Bible a 'name' stands for the whole person — his identity, his character, and above all his authority. To do or say something 'in someone's name' is to act on his behalf, as his representative, by his authority — the way an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king's, or a constable says 'stop, in the name of the law.' So when the apostles 'spoke in the name of Jesus,' they were not merely mentioning him; they were publicly proclaiming who he is — the crucified and risen Lord — and calling people to trust and obey him, and doing it as his authorized messengers, backed by his authority and not their own (as when the lame man was healed 'in the name of Jesus Christ,' 3:6, and 'there is salvation in no one else,' 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the authoritative announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

It is worth knowing what the sentence actually was, because English translations pass over it in three words. The synagogue flogging was forty strokes less one — the law permitted forty and the practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break it (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The man was stripped to the waist and bent over, and the strokes were laid on with a leather scourge, a third of them on the chest and the rest across the back. Men were carried away from it. Paul, who received the same punishment five separate times, thought it worth listing among the things that nearly killed him (2 Corinthians 11:24). This is not a formality or a caution. Eleven men left that chamber unable to stand straight.

And notice the incoherence of what has just happened, because it is the most damning thing in the chapter. Minutes earlier the council was warned by its most honoured member that it might be found fighting against God. It accepted the advice. Then it had the men beaten and told them again to stop speaking. A body that genuinely thought it might be opposing the Almighty had one reasonable course and did not take it. They kept the verdict and lowered the sentence, which is what men do when they have decided the question already and are only negotiating the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven men walk out of the Sanhedrin with their backs opened, and Luke says they were rejoicing. Not resigned. Not composed. Not bearing it well. Rejoicing, on the way home, out loud enough that somebody remembered it.

And the reason he gives is a sentence that should not be able to exist: they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour. Two words that cannot stand together. To be counted worthy is to be honoured, singled out, judged fit for something valuable; dishonour is public shame, the thing every man in that culture organised his life to avoid. Luke welds them. Whatever had happened to these men, it had reversed the sign on the whole transaction. They walked into that room as defendants and came out feeling that they had been given something. Not long before, this same group had been arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest. The argument is over. The prize turned out to be a flogging.

Then the phrase that ought to stop a reader: for the Name. That is all Luke writes. No qualifier, no possessive, nothing to say whose name is meant. Every Jew reading it would feel the weight of that construction, because in Jewish speech the Name was how you referred to the God of Israel when you would not pronounce the divine name itself. And here is Luke, writing about a carpenter executed six weeks earlier outside the city wall, and he uses the phrase absolutely, as though there could be no confusion about which name is meant. Among these people there was not. The council in this very chapter refused to say the name at all, calling him this man (v. 28); the apostles have stopped needing to say it, for the opposite reason.

Now a guard is needed here, because this verse has been laid on suffering people as a demand, and it is not one. Three things keep it honest. First, they are not rejoicing in the pain; they are rejoicing in what the pain meant — that the Lord they had abandoned in a garden had now counted them fit to be shamed on his account. Nobody is asked to enjoy a scourge. Second, this is a specific kind of suffering: dishonour incurred for Christ, in the course of obeying him. A diagnosis is not dishonour for the Name. Neither is a bereavement, a betrayal, or a depression that will not lift. Those are real and Scripture speaks to them elsewhere and at length; this verse is not the text to beat a grieving person with. Third, this joy is a thing given, not manufactured. It arrived in them on the way out of that building. It is not a mood that a Christian owes in advance and is failing to produce.

And to anyone who reads this and quietly concludes he could never do it — that if it cost him his job, his family's standing, or a beating, he would fold — look at who is walking out of that chamber. The man in front is Peter. Seven weeks ago, with nothing at stake but a servant girl's opinion beside a fire, he swore he had never met Jesus, and then went out and wept. Nobody in history has a worse record under pressure than the man leading this procession. What changed was not his temperament. Something was given to him that had not been there in the courtyard, and it is given to people when it is needed and not before. The measure of what you could bear today is not the measure of what you would be carried through tomorrow.

Luke ends the chapter with the council's order and its answer set side by side. They were charged not to speak in the name of Jesus. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus. Every day — not resumed after a decent interval, but daily, from that day. In the temple, which is the most public and most dangerous place in the city, and belongs to the men who ordered the flogging; and house to house, at kitchen tables, where the church has always done most of its real work. Both together, and neither instead of the other.

They did not cease. It is a strange note to end on, and it is the right one. The whole apparatus of the most powerful religious body in the world had been brought to bear on eleven provincials over two days — arrest, imprisonment, formal trial, corporal punishment, legal injunction — and by the following morning the only measurable result was that the message was being preached in more houses than before. He is worth this, was the verdict of the men with the wounds. Two thousand years later the name they would not stop saying is spoken every hour in every language on earth, and nobody can tell you the name of a single man who sat on the council that day.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church five weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; the next verse tells us that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The church is growing — and growth creates problems. The Hellenist widows are being neglected in the daily distribution. This is not a scandal; it is what happens when an organism grows faster than its structures can accommodate. The twelve could try to do everything. Instead they do something remarkable: they name the problem plainly, they define their own calling with precision (“we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the Word”), and they delegate to men of character and Spirit.

The result is instructive: “the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem.” When the church’s structures serve the Word rather than compete with it, the Word runs. Ministry organisation is not bureaucracy — it is stewardship of the mission.

But Luke also introduces Stephen, and with Stephen the chapter darkens. He is full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and power. He does wonders no one can deny. He speaks with a wisdom the opposition cannot withstand. So they do what those who cannot win an argument always do: they lie. And Stephen, standing before the council with false witnesses arrayed against him, has a face like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first organizational crisis in the church is also the first demonstration of the church's Spirit-guided wisdom. A complaint arises: the Hellenistic Jewish widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The complaint is not theological but administrative — a failure of pastoral care that threatens the church's unity across its cultural divide. The apostles' response is both principled and practical: they will not abandon the ministry of the Word and prayer for table service, but they will ensure that table service receives Spirit-filled, wisdom-endowed leadership of its own.

The appointment of the Seven is not merely organizational efficiency; it is a theological act. Seven men, all with Greek names, all apparently from the Hellenistic Jewish community that felt overlooked, are set apart by prayer and the laying on of hands. The community that felt marginalized receives representation in leadership. And the result: the word of God continued to increase, the number of disciples multiplied greatly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' insistence that they must not 'give up preaching the word of God to serve tables' (v. 2) is not a hierarchy of dignity but a principle of vocation. Every member of the body is called to a specific ministry; the body is impoverished when people are given tasks that prevent them from fulfilling their God-given calling. The Seven are not 'junior ministers' — Stephen will prove to be one of the most theologically powerful figures in Acts. But their calling is to table service, and that calling is as Spirit-endowed as the apostolic calling to the word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The organizational problem threatened to divide the church along cultural lines (Hebrew vs Hellenistic Jews). The Spirit-guided solution served the marginalized community by placing them in leadership. Now: Every church must wrestle with the question of who is being overlooked in its pastoral care — and the answer always involves the Spirit-filled appointment of the right people to the right ministries.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary: The complaint surfaces at the intersection of rapid growth and cultural difference: Hellenistic Jewish widows (Greek-speaking, from the Diaspora) are being overlooked compared to Hebrew-speaking widows. The oversight may be unintentional — the product of language barriers and the expanding scale of the community — but its effect is to create a have and have-not division along ethnic lines. The twelve's response is principled: the ministry of the word cannot be sacrificed for administrative needs, but administrative needs cannot be neglected either. Both are genuine callings; neither can absorb the other.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this task. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The qualifications the twelve require for table service — 'good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom' — are not lesser than the qualifications for preaching. Every ministry that represents Christ to the community requires the Spirit and wisdom; the only difference is the specific form the service takes. The apostles' insistence on their own 'prayer and the ministry of the word' is not a claim of superiority but a recognition of vocation: they are called to these specific ministries, and the community is impoverished if they abandon them for tasks others can fulfill. (cf. 1 Tim. 4:13; 2 Tim. 4:2)

Anyone who belongs to a church that elects deacons will want to know whether this is where they come from. The answer is yes and no, and the distinction is worth having. Luke never calls these men deacons. The noun is not used of them here or anywhere else; later he simply calls Philip one of the seven (21:8). What is used, twice and pointedly, is the word underneath it: the apostles will not give up the service of the word in order to serve tables. Both halves of that sentence are the same root, and that is the whole argument. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, a menial one and a spiritual one. They are two forms of the one thing, and the only question is which one a particular man is called to.

So the church has always been right to see the seed of the office here, and Paul's later requirements for deacons — men of dignity, tested, holding the faith with a clear conscience (1 Tim. 3:8-13) — plainly grow from the same soil as the qualifications set out in this verse. But do not reduce these seven to an administrative committee. Watch what they actually do next. Stephen is arguing in synagogues within a paragraph and is dead within a chapter. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, baptises an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. Neither of them stayed at the tables. Whatever the church later made of the office, it began with men so full of the Spirit that the job could not hold them.

And notice what the first appointment in the history of the church was actually for. Not a building programme, not a doctrinal commission, not a mission board. Some widows who spoke the wrong language were being missed at the food distribution, and the apostles treated that as serious enough to reorganise the leadership of the church over it. That is worth sitting with. The complaint came from the minority group, and the solution handed the entire operation to seven men with Greek names. They did not manage the grievance; they gave the aggrieved the keys.

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All seven names are Greek — the community addressed the Hellenistic complaint by putting Hellenistic leaders in charge of the distribution: practical wisdom guided by the Spirit, honouring the marginalized by entrusting leadership to them. The apostles' laying on of hands publicly commissions and sets them apart, with prayer for the Spirit's empowering. Stephen is at once distinguished — 'full of faith and of the Holy Spirit' — and will not stay a table-server long; the Spirit fills people to overflow.

'Full of faith and of the Holy Spirit' — but how could anyone tell? The apostles told the church to pick out such men (v. 3), so the fullness was no hidden claim but something the congregation could recognise. It shows itself, and over time unmistakably. In character — the fruit the Spirit grows: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control (Gal. 5:22–23), steady enough to earn 'good repute.' In wisdom — how a man speaks and handles matters (Stephen's, which his opponents 'could not withstand,' v. 10). In faith, a settled trust and boldness; and soon, in Stephen, in grace and power, 'great wonders and signs' (v. 8), even a face shining 'like the face of an angel' (v. 15). The church needed no special revelation; they saw the Spirit in how he lived, spoke, and served — Jesus' own rule, 'you will recognise them by their fruits' (Matt. 7:16, 20). And note the lovely ordinariness: these Spirit-filled men were chosen to wait tables and settle a food dispute; fullness of the Spirit is proved first in humble, everyday service, not only the spectacular.

'They prayed and laid their hands on them.' The Bible uses this gesture several ways, best read against its Old Testament roots: for blessing (Jacob over Ephraim and Manasseh, Gen. 48:14; Jesus over the children, Mark 10:16); for identifying with a sacrifice (the worshipper's hand on the animal, Lev. 1:4; the high priest's on the scapegoat, Lev. 16:21); and, closest here, for commissioning to an office. The pattern is Moses and Joshua: 'Take Joshua... a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him... and commission him' (Num. 27:18–20), so that afterward 'Joshua... was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him' (Deut. 34:9). Just so here: the seven are publicly set apart, with prayer that God would equip them by his Spirit. The New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry — Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3), Timothy's gift given 'when the council of elders laid their hands on you' (1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6). Two things to hold: it is never magic — always joined to prayer, and it is the prayer that asks God to act; and it is a public act, the church openly recognising those God has called. (Scripture even warns against doing it lightly: 'do not be hasty in the laying on of hands,' 1 Tim. 5:22.)

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: The organizational solution produces spiritual fruitfulness: word increase, disciple multiplication, and — most dramatically — 'a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.' The priests who served in the temple at whose gates the lame man was healed, in whose courts the apostles taught, are now submitting themselves to the gospel. The word 'obedient' is significant: faith is not merely intellectual assent but the submission of the whole self to the authority of the risen Lord. The gospel is penetrating the very heart of the religious establishment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Stephen refuses to stay in his lane. Appointed to distribute food, he moves immediately into public disputation and Spirit-powered signs and wonders — because the Spirit who fills him is the Spirit of proclamation, and no organizational category can contain him. The opposition he encounters is instructive: when his opponents cannot win the argument (they 'could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking'), they do what every movement that cannot defeat truth does: they manufacture false witnesses and drag him before the council on invented charges.

The false witnesses' accusation is a distorted version of a truth: Stephen has been speaking about Jesus changing the Mosaic customs and the temple. He has been — and he is right to do so. The old order of temple and Torah is giving way to the new order of the Spirit and the fulfillment of all that the temple and Torah pointed toward. Stephen's face shines like an angel: this is not allegory but theophanic reality — the man who is about to die for the gospel is already reflecting the glory of the Lord he is going to see.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest and trial follow the exact pattern of Jesus's arrest and trial: false witnesses, charges of blasphemy against the temple and the law, the council's rage. This is not coincidence — it is the pattern of all prophetic witness that challenges entrenched religious power. The servant is not above the master. Reformed theology sees in Stephen's fate the confirmation that genuine gospel proclamation will always meet the resistance of those whose power depends on the maintenance of the status quo that the gospel overturns.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom but refused to yield to it — so they resorted to violence and false testimony. The gospel will not always win the argument in the short term; sometimes it wins the martyr's crown first. Now: The church is called to the same quality of Spirit-and-wisdom witness that Stephen embodied, knowing that the outcome is in God's hands and that even martyrdom is not defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen refuses to stay in his administrative lane. The Spirit who fills him for table service is the Spirit of proclamation, and that Spirit cannot be contained by an organizational role. 'Full of grace and power' — the grace that marks his character and the power that accompanies his ministry are both gifts of the same Spirit who appointed him to distribute bread.

What does 'full of grace and power' mean? It is the third time Luke describes Stephen with 'full of...' (full of faith and the Spirit, v. 5; of the Spirit and wisdom, v. 3; now of grace and power) — he is a man saturated by God. Grace (charis) carries two notes that belong together: the favour of God resting richly upon him — his life freely enabled and blessed by God, nothing of it earned — and the graciousness that such favour produces, the winsome, Christlike attractiveness of a man shaped by grace (the same word lies behind Jesus' 'gracious words,' Luke 4:22, and 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14). Power (dynamis) is the Spirit's enabling might — the very power Jesus promised, 'you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you' (Acts 1:8) — here overflowing in 'great wonders and signs.' Note the order: grace first, then power. The favour and gracious character come first, and the power flows out of a life already full of grace; power without grace is a dangerous thing, but Stephen had both. And mark who this is: not an apostle, but one of the seven chosen to wait on tables (vv. 3–5) — yet full of grace and power and working wonders that Luke had until now reported of the apostles alone (2:43; 5:12). The grace and power of God were never the private property of the Twelve; they filled a humble table-servant who was wholly yielded to the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first mention of a synagogue in Acts, so a word on what it was. The synagogue (Greek synagōgē, simply 'a gathering') was the local Jewish assembly and meeting-house — not the temple (there was only one temple, in Jerusalem), but a community centre found in every town and city where Jews lived, for the reading and study of Scripture, prayer, and teaching. It arose after the Babylonian exile, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were scattered, and by Jesus' and Paul's day it was the heartbeat of Jewish life everywhere. (For its origins, how a synagogue service ran, and whether Jews still gather so today, see the fuller note at 13:15.) A great city like Jerusalem held many synagogues, often grouped by homeland or language — which brings us to this one.

'The synagogue of the Freedmen' — who were these opponents? 'Freedmen' (Libertinoi, a Latin word, libertini) means freed slaves and their descendants. The likeliest background is that these were Jews, or the children of Jews, who had been taken captive — many when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC — carried off to Rome as slaves, later set free, and whose families formed a distinct community; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. Jerusalem held many such synagogues for Greek-speaking Jews of the diaspora, and Luke names several homelands here: Cyrene (North Africa), Alexandria (Egypt), and Cilicia and Asia (regions of Asia Minor). (Whether this means one synagogue or two or more is grammatically uncertain; the number is not the point.)
