On this view the regular doctrine of how we receive the Spirit is taught in the letters, not drawn from these one-time narratives — and there the answer is plain: the Spirit is given to all who believe, at conversion ('anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him,' Rom. 8:9; 'when you believed, you were sealed,' Eph. 1:13; Gal. 3:2). So you need not fear you are a half-Christian awaiting a second gift: if you belong to Christ, you already have the Spirit. The point is said with respect for brothers who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon's request unmasks what his 'belief' was: he wants the Spirit-conferring power as a commodity, something he can acquire with money and deploy for his own ministry. 'Give me this power also' — the word 'power' (exousia) reveals his framework: he thinks in terms of power-transfer, not personal transformation. Money can buy what magicians sell; but the Spirit of God is not for sale, and the apostles are not vendors. Simon's request is the paradigmatic error of treating the gifts of God as products in an economy of religious exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's response is severe and clear: 'may your silver perish with you.' The condemnation is not of wealth but of the attempt to commodify what is freely given by God. 'You have neither part nor lot in this matter' — Simon's offer reveals that he has no share in what he is trying to buy. His heart is 'not right before God' — not aligned with the truth of the gospel, not transformed by the grace he has professed. The word 'simony' (purchasing church offices) derives from this episode, naming the perennial temptation to treat God's gifts as marketable goods.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter does not give up on Simon — he calls him to repentance. The 'if possible' of v. 22 is not uncertainty about God's forgiveness but an honest recognition that Simon must actually repent, not merely regret the rebuke. 'The gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity' — Peter diagnoses Simon's spiritual condition: a heart that has not been liberated by the gospel but is still bound by its own agenda and bitterness. The call to repentance is still open; Simon is not beyond grace. His response (vv. 24–25) is ambiguous — he asks Peter to pray for him but makes no visible turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon's response focuses on the consequences rather than the repentance: 'that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.' He does not say 'I repent' or 'forgive me'; he asks for intercession against judgment. Luke leaves his story unresolved — a warning to readers not to mistake religious amazement and formal baptism for genuine faith. Peter and John, their apostolic mission complete, return to Jerusalem — but not before 'preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.' The Spirit who uses persecution to scatter the church uses the apostles' journey home to seed an entire region.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit who called Philip to Samaria now calls him away from the most successful revival he has ever experienced, to a desert road, to meet a single man — one of the most deliberately provocative scenes in Acts. An Ethiopian eunuch, a Gentile court official of the queen of Ethiopia, returning from worship at Jerusalem with a scroll of Isaiah in his hands, cannot understand what he is reading. Philip is sent to explain it. The explanation leads to baptism, to joy, and to the eunuch's departure — and Philip is immediately transported to another city. The encounter is over almost before it begins.

The eunuch is reading Isaiah 53 — the Servant Song that describes the suffering and death of the one who bore the sins of the many. Philip begins with this very text and preaches Jesus from it. The question the eunuch asks — 'Who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?' — is the hermeneutical question that unlocks the entire Old Testament. The answer is Jesus, and from that answer, faith flows, the gospel is confessed, baptism follows, and joy fills the Ethiopian official on his way home to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Substitutionary Atonement

Philip begins with Isaiah 53 and 'told him the good news about Jesus.' Isaiah 53 is the clearest Old Testament anticipation of substitutionary atonement: 'he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed' (Isaiah 53:5). The Reformed tradition has always seen here the doctrinal heart of the gospel: the innocent Servant bearing the punishment deserved by the guilty, so that the guilty might go free. Philip preaches the crucified and risen Jesus from the text that most clearly explained why he had to die.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An Ethiopian eunuch — excluded from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 — is baptized and welcomed into the community of Christ. The gospel dismantles the exclusions of the old covenant in its very first Gentile encounter. Now: The gospel continues to reach those who have been told they are too far away, too different, too excluded. No distance is too great, no background too foreign, no exclusion too definitive for the Spirit who pursues the one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel's instruction is precise and apparently impractical: leave Samaria's revival for a desert road. Philip obeys at once — 'he rose and went.' The eunuch's identity is carefully drawn: Ethiopian (the end of the known world), eunuch (excluded from the assembly, Deut. 23:1), court official (a man of power), pilgrim to Jerusalem (a God-fearer drawn to Israel's worship). He is at once a man of privilege and a man of exclusion — and the gospel is about to address both.

'An angel of the Lord said to Philip' — and many a believer quietly wishes God would guide him so directly. Why was this common then but not now? First, a correction: angelic appearances were never everyday, even in Scripture. Across two thousand years they cluster at a few pivotal moments — the patriarchs, the Exodus, the prophets here and there, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, the launch of the church. Most godly saints never saw or heard an angel; they fill the narrative because Scripture records the turning points, not the ordinary years.

And Acts is exactly such a turning point: the once-for-all launch of the gospel from Jerusalem to Samaria, to this Ethiopian, to Cornelius (ch. 10), to the ends of the earth. For that foundational breakout God used extraordinary steering — angels, visions, the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9) — driving the apostles into territory they would never have entered on their own. Like the authenticating signs (see on 5:12), this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Eph. 2:20), which by nature is laid once.

Today God guides by settled and sufficient means — and we are not less supplied but more. We hold what the early church was still receiving: the completed Scripture, 'a lamp to my feet' (Ps. 119:105), able to make us 'complete, equipped for every good work' (2 Tim. 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; and prayer, wisdom, godly counsel, and providence. Scripture even warns against craving angelic encounters — against the 'worship of angels' by those who do not hold fast to Christ the Head (Col. 2:18), noting that Satan 'disguises himself as an angel of light' (2 Cor. 11:14), and that even 'if an angel from heaven' preached another gospel he is to be rejected (Gal. 1:8). Deepest of all, God 'has in these last days spoken to us by his Son' (Heb. 1:1–2), far superior to angels (Heb. 1:4); to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is to ask for something lesser. We 'walk by faith, not by sight' (2 Cor. 5:7), and 'blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' (John 20:29).

Two honest qualifications. Angels are not idle — they remain 'ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation' (Heb. 1:14), often unseen; God has not lost his freedom to use them. And no verse says outright that angels stopped speaking after the apostles; that they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a fair inference from the foundational character of the Acts era, the sufficiency of Scripture, and the Bible's own warnings. The settled point: do not hanker after an angel — you have the finished Word of God, the Spirit of God, and the Son of God himself. That is more, not less, than a voice from the desert road.

What was a 'eunuch'? Plainly, a man who had been castrated. In ancient royal courts such men were deliberately employed — above all to guard the king's or queen's household and women, since a man who could neither father children nor pose a dynastic threat was reckoned uniquely safe. Far from lowly, eunuchs often rose to the highest posts of trust — chamberlains, treasurers — like this man, 'in charge of all the treasure' of Candace. (The word could also be a looser title for a high official whatever his state — Potiphar is called a 'eunuch' though married, Gen. 39:1; and Jesus names three kinds, Matt. 19:12. Here, given his office and the exclusion below, he is most likely a literal eunuch.)

And here is the poignancy. Under the law, 'no one whose... male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD' (Deut. 23:1) — a eunuch was, by his very body, barred from full membership in Israel's worship, however earnestly he sought God. So here is a man who has travelled the length of the known world to worship in Jerusalem, only to remain an outsider, shut out at the door. Yet he is reading Isaiah — the very book where God promised the day when the eunuch who holds fast his covenant would receive 'a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off' (Isa. 56:3–5). The gospel Philip is about to preach is that promise fulfilled: in Christ the excluded outsider is brought all the way in.

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit directs Philip with specific precision: 'Go over and join this chariot.' Not 'go to that general area' but 'go to that chariot, that man, that scroll.' Divine providence has arranged the encounter: the eunuch is reading Isaiah at the exact moment Philip arrives; the Spirit gives Philip the exact instruction he needs. The Spirit's personal, specific direction of Philip to the eunuch is the pattern of all genuine mission: the Spirit goes ahead, prepares the heart, and then sends the messenger with exact timing.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip runs — the urgency of the Spirit's direction expressed in physical movement. The question 'Do you understand what you are reading?' is both honest and winsome: it acknowledges the difficulty of the text without condescension. The eunuch's response is the most teachable answer in Acts: 'How can I, unless someone guides me?' He knows his need; he welcomes help; he invites Philip into his chariot. Humility about one's understanding of Scripture is the posture that opens the door to genuine encounter with Christ in the text.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 53:7–8 — the center of the Servant Song that describes the one who dies silently, unjustly, and vicariously. 'He opens not his mouth' — the silence of the Servant before his accusers is the silence of the one who has accepted the cup the Father has given him. 'In his humiliation justice was denied him' — the death of the Servant is a miscarriage of justice by human courts; but it is the perfect justice of God, who is punishing the sins of others in the Servant. The eunuch is reading the text that explains the cross before Philip arrives to show him the text is about Jesus. (cf. Isa. 53:7–8; 1 Pet. 2:22–25)

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" And Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eunuch's question is the hermeneutical question that unlocks the entire Old Testament: is the Servant someone in particular, or is this a general picture? Philip's answer begins 'with this Scripture' — Isaiah 53 — and from it preaches Jesus. The christological interpretation of the Servant Songs is not imported into Isaiah but drawn from Isaiah: the Servant's silence, humiliation, vicarious suffering, and death by injustice are fulfilled in Jesus's passion in a way that no other figure in history has fulfilled them. Jesus is not a projection onto Isaiah; Isaiah is a prophecy of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'What prevents me from being baptized?' — a remarkable question, given that the eunuch's own body was the legal answer under the old covenant (Deuteronomy 23:1). But Philip's question in response ('if you believe with all your heart, you may') establishes the gospel's single condition: faith. The eunuch's confession — 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God' — is the earliest baptismal confession in Acts and one of the most comprehensive: he affirms both the messianic identity ('Christ') and the divine identity ('Son of God') of Jesus. Nothing prevents his baptism.

What makes this scene so charged is where the eunuch has been reading. He has a scroll of Isaiah open to chapter 53 when Philip arrives — the Servant's vicarious suffering and death. But just three chapters later, Isaiah 56:3–5 makes the eunuch a figure of prophetic promise: let not the eunuch say, I am a dry tree; for thus says the LORD, to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters. The very book the eunuch is reading contains the prophecy that he — the excluded one — will be gathered. He is not merely reading Isaiah 53; he is inhabiting Isaiah 56. Luke wants his readers to feel the precision of Providence: the Spirit does not just send Philip to the right road but to the right man reading the right book at the right passage.

One thing about verse 37 needs saying plainly, because your Bible may not have it. Many modern translations print verse 36 and then jump straight to verse 38, with the exchange about believing with all your heart pushed down into a footnote — which makes for a puzzling gap in the numbering if nobody explains it. The reason is that the words are missing from the earliest and best copies of Acts. They are old: Irenaeus is quoting them before the end of the second century. But they read exactly like the question and answer the early church used at the water's edge, and a scribe who knew that liturgy by heart would very naturally have supplied what looked to him like a missing line.

Nothing is lost if it goes. The eunuch plainly did believe — he asks for baptism himself, and he goes on his way rejoicing — and every word the verse contains is taught openly elsewhere in the same book: repent and be baptised (2:38), they believed and were baptised (8:12), believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, and he was baptised at once (16:31-33). So no doctrine rests on it, and no doctrine is damaged by it. What the sentence preserves, even if the hand that wrote it was not Luke's, is an accurate photograph of what the church asked a man before it took him down into the water. The words may be a later copyist's. The practice they describe is apostolic.

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The baptism is complete, and Philip is immediately transported by the Spirit — the encounter is over, and the human intermediary departs. The eunuch's response is the same as the crowd at Pentecost's response, the same as Samaria's response: joy. The gospel always produces joy in those who genuinely receive it, because it announces the arrival of the one who is the fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11). The eunuch returns to Ethiopia with no church, no Bible in his language, no pastor — only the Spirit and the risen Christ. And tradition says the Ethiopian church began with him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip is transported to Azotus (the ancient Philistine city of Ashdod) and continues evangelizing up the coastal plain to Caesarea, the major Roman port city where he will eventually settle (21:8). The Spirit who removes him from the eunuch sends him immediately into new mission territory. Philip's life is a model of Spirit-directed mission: obedient to sudden redirections, faithful in revival and in desert encounter, content to disappear from one story so the next chapter of God's mission can begin.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
No conversion in history has been more dramatic, more sovereign, or more consequential. Saul of Tarsus is not seeking God. He is hunting God’s people — breathing threats and murder, armed with letters of arrest, heading to Damascus to drag more believers to prison. And the risen Christ stops him on the road. A light from heaven. A voice. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Not them — me. To touch the church is to touch Christ. The head and the body are one.

What happens to Saul on the Damascus road is not the result of prior openness, spiritual preparation, or moral readiness. It is pure, sovereign, unilateral grace — the kind that stops a man in the middle of his worst act and makes him a new creature. Saul does not choose Christ; Christ chooses Saul. “He is a chosen instrument of mine.” The word is skeuos eklogēs — vessel of election — and it is the language of sovereign divine appointment. The most violent persecutor of the church becomes its most prolific apostle. Only God could write that story.

And then there is Ananias — a small man in a small house on a street called Straight, who hears the Lord say “go to Saul of Tarsus” and who goes, against every instinct of self-preservation, and calls the man who had come to arrest him “Brother Saul.” Two words that cost everything and mean everything. Grace in the mouth of a frightened disciple.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The conversion of Saul of Tarsus is the most dramatic reversal in the New Testament outside of the resurrection itself. The man who superintended Stephen's execution and was 'ravaging the church' (8:3) is arrested by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, blinded, led into the city helpless, and three days later emerges as the most committed missionary the world has ever seen. Luke tells the story three times in Acts (here, in Paul's defense before the crowd in ch. 22, and before Agrippa in ch. 26) because it is the event that shapes everything that follows: the Gentile mission, the theology of grace, and the entire second half of Acts.

The encounter on the Damascus road is stark and absolute: 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' The risen Christ identifies himself with the church he is persecuting — to persecute the church is to persecute Jesus. And then the identification in reverse: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' The Christology is radical: the exalted Lord so thoroughly identifies with his people that violence against them is violence against him personally. Saul's three days of blindness, fasting, and prayer are his death and resurrection before baptism: the old Saul — the Pharisee, the persecutor, the man confident in his own righteousness — dies in the darkness, and the new creation emerges when Ananias restores his sight.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of the sovereignty of grace. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He had no inclination toward the gospel; he was destroying the church. He was not moving toward faith; he was moving toward Damascus to imprison believers. And then the risen Christ stopped him — entirely, unilaterally, sovereignly. Reformed theology sees in Saul's conversion the paradigm of all conversion: every person who comes to faith is someone who was, in one degree or another, moving away from God when God arrested them. The grace that reached Saul reaches all who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was asked to go to 'the man who has done much evil to your saints in Jerusalem.' He went — and addressed him as 'Brother Saul.' The man who could have been his executioner became his brother. Now: The gospel creates family out of former enemies. The church's testimony to the grace that reached Saul is its most powerful argument for the gospel's transforming power: if Christ can reach the chief of sinners, he can reach anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Still breathing threats and murder' — the participle conveys that Saul's hostility is his constant condition, not an occasional impulse. He has not moderated since Stephen's stoning; he has intensified. The request for letters to the Damascus synagogues reveals both the geographical reach of his persecution and the legal structure through which he operated: the high priest's authority extended to Jewish communities throughout the Diaspora. 'The Way' — the earliest self-designation of the Christian movement, emphasizing that following Jesus is a path, a manner of life, not merely a set of beliefs.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him' — the glory of the risen Christ, brighter than the Syrian midday sun (26:13). Saul falls to the ground: the posture of prostration before overwhelming divine presence. The double name — 'Saul, Saul' — echoes the divine address of Abraham (Genesis 22:11), Moses (Exodus 3:4), and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10): the urgent, personal summons of God to a specific individual at a turning-point moment. 'Why are you persecuting me?' — Jesus does not ask why Saul is persecuting the church; he asks why Saul is persecuting him. The identification is total. (cf. 1 Cor. 15:8–10; Gal. 1:15–16)

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Who are you, Lord?' — Saul addresses the voice as Lord before he knows whose voice it is; the light and the fall have already produced a posture of submission. The answer is the most important sentence in Saul's life: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' The Jesus he has been persecuting is alive, is Lord, is the risen Christ. In a moment, everything Saul has built his life on — the law, the Pharisaic tradition, his own righteousness — is overturned. 'Rise and enter the city' — the sovereign Lord who has arrested him now directs his next steps. Saul will be told what to do: his autonomy is over.

A note for anyone reading alongside an older Bible. The King James adds a sentence here that modern versions do not print: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks, along with Saul's trembling question about what the Lord would have him do. The words are genuine — Jesus really did say them, and Luke records them when Paul retells the scene before Agrippa (26:14) — but they are not in the Greek manuscripts at this point. A copyist, knowing the fuller version from chapter 26, filled them in here. So nothing has been lost from Scripture; the saying has simply been returned to the place where Luke actually put it. The image itself is worth keeping: a goad was the farmer's spiked stick, and an ox that kicked back at it only drove the point deeper. Saul had been kicking for a while.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The companions hear the voice but see no one — they are witnesses to the supernatural character of the event without being recipients of its content. Their speechlessness is the appropriate response to a theophany they cannot interpret. Saul's blindness is the physical enactment of his spiritual condition: the man most certain he could see clearly — the zealous Pharisee, righteous by the law's standards — now sees nothing and is led by the hand like a dependent child. The reversal is total and immediate.

The first half of verse 7 has been a favourite of sceptics for a long time, and it deserves a straight answer. Luke says here that the men were hearing the voice but seeing no one. When Paul himself tells the story later in this same book, he says that those with him saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9). Same author, same book, same event, and on the face of it a flat contradiction — which is why it turns up in every list of Bible errors ever compiled.

It dissolves in the Greek, and not by special pleading. The verb for hearing takes its object in different cases with different senses: with one case it means to hear a sound, with the other to hear with understanding — much as we distinguish hearing someone from catching what they said. Luke uses the first construction here and the second at 22:9. So the two sentences are saying precisely what any of us would say about the same afternoon: the men heard a noise but could not make out the words. Modern translations show this openly — the ESV renders 22:9 did not understand the voice — and the difficulty simply disappears.

The seeing works the same way. They saw the light, which is why they were struck speechless; they did not see the person who spoke, which is why Luke says they saw no one. And notice the pastoral point sitting underneath the grammar. The men beside him experienced the identical event — the same blaze, the same sound, the same road — and went away with nothing but a story about strange weather. Saul went away with a Lord. Proximity to revelation is not the same as receiving it, and the difference between the two was not in the light but in whom it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three days without sight, food, or drink: the posture of one in crisis, in prayer, at the end of himself. The three days anticipate the death-and-resurrection pattern of baptism: the old Saul — the Pharisee, the persecutor — is dying in the darkness, and the new creation will emerge when Ananias comes. Fasting intensifies prayer; the darkness forces inward the attention that had previously been turned outward in confident self-reliance. God is at work in Saul's three-day night.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The risen Christ is orchestrating the encounter from both ends simultaneously. Ananias's response — 'Here I am, Lord' — is the posture of Isaiah (6:8) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4): the servant available for whatever the Lord assigns. The precision of the directions — street, house, name, city — is characteristic of the Spirit's guidance throughout Acts. The Lord tells Ananias what Saul is doing: praying. The man who entered Damascus in authority to arrest believers is now a blind man in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord has already shown Saul in a vision that Ananias is coming — the healing has been previewed for the one who will receive it. This double orchestration — directing Ananias to Saul, and showing Saul that Ananias is coming — ensures that both participants understand they are being brought together by divine arrangement, not human coincidence. When Ananias arrives, Saul will be expecting him. The Spirit's work in preparation always exceeds the missionary's awareness of what has been prepared.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary: Ananias's objection is reasonable and understandable: Saul's reputation has preceded him. 'How much evil he has done to your saints' — the saints, the holy ones, the community to which Ananias himself belongs. And Saul is not only a past persecutor; he has authority to arrest 'all who call on your name' — including Ananias himself. Going to Saul is, by any rational calculation, walking into the arms of the man who is hunting you. Ananias's honesty with God is itself a form of faith: he raises the objection, but he will go when the Lord answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord's answer to Ananias's objection contains the two most important facts about Saul's future: he is a 'chosen instrument' (divine election, not human decision) to carry the name before Gentiles, kings, and Israel (the scope of Acts 9–28); and he 'must suffer' (his suffering for the name will be proportionate to his former infliction of suffering in the name's suppression). The call to mission and the call to suffering are inseparable in Acts and in Paul's own letters (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The Lord does not conceal the cost from the one he is calling. (cf. Rom. 1:1; 2 Cor. 11:23–27)

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Brother Saul' — the first word Ananias speaks is 'brother.' The man who came to arrest members of the Way is welcomed by one of them as family. This is the gospel's social miracle: the persecutor becomes the brother. The healing and the Spirit come together: sight returns, the Spirit fills, and Saul is baptized. The three days of blindness, prayer, and fasting are over; the new creation emerges from the baptismal water. Paul will later call his conversion a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17) and a participation in Christ's death and resurrection (Galatians 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, He is the Son of God.' — the theological content of Saul's first proclamation is the highest possible christological claim: 'Son of God.' This is not a gradual dawning of insight; it is the immediate consequence of meeting the risen Christ. The man who was going to the Damascus synagogues to arrest believers goes to the Damascus synagogues to preach the faith he had been destroying. The reversal is total and instant. The christology that will undergird all of Paul's letters is already fully formed: Jesus is the Son of God. (cf. Gal. 1:16; 2 Cor. 5:17)

What did Saul mean by 'Son of God'? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God's own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God — which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with 'making himself equal with God' because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). 'Son' here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father's humanity, the divine Son shares the Father's deity, eternally — of one substance with him, 'begotten, not made.' Second, 'Son of God' was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David's line was called God's son (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7), so to say 'Jesus is the Son of God' is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King — which is just where Saul's preaching goes next, 'proving that Jesus was the Christ' (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers 'sons of God' (Job 1:6; John 1:12) — but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the Son, the 'only-begotten' (monogenēs, John 3:16), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience — and it is the very confession that saves, 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name' (John 20:31; cf. 1 John 4:15). And here is the wonder of the moment: the man who had set out to destroy everyone who made this claim is now the first in Damascus to make it.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound to the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Damascus synagogue's bewilderment is understandable: Saul is doing the opposite of what he came to do. 'Increased all the more in strength' — the opposition that should have silenced him energizes him. 'Confounded' — the word implies a complete defeat in argument; Saul's combination of rabbinic training, personal encounter with the risen Christ, and Spirit-given understanding of Scripture makes him effectively unanswerable. The persecutor has become the most formidable advocate for the faith he once destroyed.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary: Saul's first experience of persecution is at the hands of the same community he once served. The plot mirrors the plots against Jesus and Stephen: when the message cannot be refuted, violence is the next resort. 'Watching the gates day and night' — the siege is thorough, the intent murderous. Paul will later mention this episode in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33 with an additional detail: the governor of Damascus was also involved, under the Nabataean king Aretas, whose ethnarch watched the city gates.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary: The escape in a basket through the city wall is both humiliating and providential. Paul will later cite it as his first 'boast' in weakness (2 Corinthians 11:30–33) — the episode that established the pattern of his entire apostolic career: not triumph but survival, not power but endurance, the treasure carried in a clay jar. The disciples who lower him over the wall are the Damascene community he has just spent time building — their care for him is the first concrete expression of the church's solidarity with its most controversial new member.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem church's fear of Saul is entirely rational: his reputation for destroying the church is intact, and his conversion claim might be a ruse. Barnabas — the 'son of encouragement' who first appeared selling his field in chapter 4 — again demonstrates his characteristic gift: seeing what others fear to see, trusting where others hesitate. His advocacy for Saul before the apostles is the bridge between the persecutor and the community he persecuted. Without Barnabas, Saul might never have been integrated into the Jerusalem church.

Set this beside Paul's own account of the same visit and a question surfaces. Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that when he finally went up to Jerusalem he saw Cephas, and stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother (Gal. 1:18-19). Plural in one, and pointedly not plural in the other.

They fit without strain once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul's reception — that the church's leadership received him, which is the whole point of the paragraph — and uses the collective term for that body, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when in fact two directors were in the office that week. Paul is under oath, so to speak: he is arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, so he counts heads with deliberate precision and keeps the number as small as honesty allows. His case depends on it having been a short and limited visit; Luke's case depends on it having happened at all. And notice that Paul's two names are exactly the two who mattered for the introduction — Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas got him in front of the men whose word would settle it.

The timing fits the same way. Read alone, Luke's account gives the impression of a swift sequence, and he does not pause to say that three years in Arabia and Damascus lie between the road and this doorway (Gal. 1:17-18; and see v. 30). That is not concealment. Luke is writing the story of a movement and moves at the pace of the movement; Paul is writing his own defence and needs the calendar. Neither of them is telling you something the other denies.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul's pattern in Jerusalem mirrors his pattern in Damascus: bold proclamation in the name of Jesus, disputation with the Hellenists (the very group that had disputed with Stephen, whose martyrdom Saul had approved), and a plot to kill him. The Hellenists cannot refute him any more than they could refute Stephen — so they resort to the same response. Saul has stepped into Stephen's role, advocating before the same opponents with the same Spirit and, apparently, the same mortal danger.

A word on who 'the Hellenists' were (their fuller profile is at 6:1 and 6:9): the term (Hellēnistai) means Greek-speaking Jews — men of the diaspora, raised in the Greek language and culture, many with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem (such as the Synagogue of the Freedmen, 6:9). The word names a person's language and culture, not his faith: in 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking Jewish believers, whereas here — as with Stephen's opponents — it means unbelieving Greek-speaking Jews. And there is a sharp irony in Saul disputing with them: a man of Tarsus in Cilicia (6:9), he was himself a Hellenist, very likely once standing with this same circle against Stephen — and now he turns to plead the name of Jesus among his own former camp, and meets the very answer Stephen met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem brothers act to protect their most controversial member: they route him through Caesarea to Tarsus, his hometown. The period in Tarsus (covering what Galatians 1:17–21 suggests was at least three years in Arabia and Syria-Cilicia) is the hidden preparation time — years of obscurity in which Paul was being formed for the mission he will carry. God does not rush his instruments; he prepares them in silence before deploying them in public. Barnabas will retrieve Saul from this obscurity in 11:25 when the Antioch church needs a teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's summary statement covers the period of relative peace after Saul's departure from Jerusalem. The church's growth is described in terms of its spiritual character: 'fear of the Lord' (the reverential awe that marks a community conscious of God's presence) and 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' (the paraklēsis — the consoling, strengthening, encouraging work of the Spirit). These two together produce multiplication: a community that fears God and is filled with the Spirit's comfort is a community the world finds both sobering and attractive.

On 'walking in the fear of the Lord,' see the fuller treatment at 5:11 — the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness (the man at the hearth, who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it). Here it is worth dwelling on its companion phrase, 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit.' The word 'comfort' (paraklēsis) is far richer than our modern notion of soothing ease. It belongs to the same family as paraklētos — the name Jesus gave the Spirit, the 'Helper' or 'Comforter' he promised: 'I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever' (John 14:16). The root means to be 'called alongside' to give aid, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and — as the old word 'comfort' (from the Latin for 'with strength') tells us — to make strong. So 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' is no cosy ease; it is the personal presence of God's own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them in trouble, embolden them to witness, and strengthen them to stand and grow. And mark the lovely pairing Luke sets down: fear and comfort, side by side — trembling reverence before the holy God, and the strong consolation of his Spirit. They are not rivals but partners; the same church that fears God is upheld by his Helper — and out of the two together it 'multiplied.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Saul is in Tarsus preparing for his mission, Peter is extending the Jerusalem church's reach through the coastal plain — the territory Philip had evangelized between Azotus and Caesarea. Two healing miracles frame this section: Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, told to rise and make his bed; and Tabitha (Dorcas), a woman full of good works and acts of charity, raised from the dead. Both miracles are performed explicitly 'in the name of Jesus Christ' or by calling on his name — the authority behind every apostolic act is the authority of the risen Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha (vv. 36–43) deliberately echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter (Luke 8:49–56): the mourners sent outside, the command 'rise,' the taking of the hand, the presentation to the community. Peter is not performing his own miracles; he is ministering in the power of the one who raised Jairus's daughter and who was himself raised from the dead. Every healing and resurrection in Acts is a preview of the final resurrection, a foretaste of the new creation in which all that sin and death have broken will be permanently restored.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Tabitha was known for 'good works and acts of charity,' and when she died, the widows she had served showed Peter the coats and garments she had made for them. Her resurrection was the answer to the prayers of a community she had served. Now: The church's ministry of practical love — clothing the poor, caring for widows, serving the marginalized — is the soil in which the witness of the gospel grows. Tabitha's deeds were the evidence of the faith that the resurrection confirmed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's itinerant ministry through the coastal communities is the apostolic equivalent of the scattered believers' missionary work — both are extending the church's reach through the movement of God's servants. Lydda (ancient Lod) is in the Shephelah region southeast of the port of Joppa. Aeneas represents the kind of need that the gospel always finds: a man defined by his condition, bedridden for a period longer than the church has existed, whose restoration will proclaim the gospel's power more effectively than a sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Jesus Christ heals you' — the healing is attributed immediately to its actual source; Peter is explicit that he is not the healer. Eight years of paralysis ended with a word spoken in the name of Jesus — 'immediately he rose.' The healing is not private: all the residents of Lydda and the Sharon plain saw Aeneas and turned to the Lord. The restored body is the sermon; the miracle is the proclamation. In every healing in Acts, the physical restoration is a concrete manifestation of the gospel's claim that Jesus is Lord over everything that sin and death have broken.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary: Tabitha's description — 'full of good works and acts of charity' — is the portrait of a disciple whose faith was expressed in practical love for the community's most vulnerable. Her name is preserved in both Aramaic (Tabitha) and Greek (Dorcas), suggesting a bilingual community that treasured her in two languages. Her death is a community catastrophe: the widows she served depended on her, and her absence leaves a gap that no organizational arrangement can fill. Luke's note that her body was washed and laid in an upper room follows Jewish burial custom and preserves the historical detail of what Peter will enter.

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' urgent summons — 'please come without delay' — is not mere hope but prayer expressed in action: they have seen what Jesus did for Jairus's daughter and Lazarus, and they dare to believe that the power that raised the dead is still at work in his church through his apostle. The geography matters: Lydda is close enough to Joppa that an urgent summons can reach Peter in time. The disciples' faith is expressed not in passive waiting but in active seeking — they go to find the person through whom God is working.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary: The widows' exhibition of the garments Tabitha made is both a tribute to her and an implicit prayer: this is what will be lost if she does not return. Peter kneels in prayer first — the miracle is not the result of apostolic authority exercised independently but of prayer addressed to the Lord who raises the dead. The scene deliberately echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter: the mourners put outside, the command 'arise,' the immediate response. 'Tabitha, arise' is almost identical in Aramaic to Jesus's 'Talitha cumi' (Mark 5:41). Peter acts in his Lord's authority and his Lord's pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her to them alive.
verseByVerse.commentary: The taking of her hand echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:41) — Peter is not merely following a technique but participating in the same redemptive action his Lord performed. 'He presented her to them alive' — the presentation is the proclamation: the community that had come to grieve receives instead the occasion of joy. The raising of Tabitha is the gospel enacted: the one who was dead is alive, the one who was lost is restored, the community that mourned now celebrates. The resurrection of Jesus has practical consequences in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary: The raising of Tabitha, like the healing of Aeneas, produces widespread faith: 'many believed in the Lord.' The miracles are not ends in themselves but proclamation in visible form; the community responds to what it has seen by turning to the one who did it. Peter's lodging with Simon the tanner is a detail Luke preserves with significance: tanners worked with dead animals and were considered ritually unclean — Peter's comfort with a tanner's hospitality hints at the attitude shift that the vision of chapter 10 will make explicit.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
The tenth chapter of Acts is one of the pivotal moments in the history of redemption. God has been preparing two men simultaneously: a Roman centurion who prays and gives alms and fears the God of Israel, and a Jewish apostle on a rooftop in Joppa having a vision that overturns a lifetime of religious instinct. The God who governs all things is coordinating these two lives across thirty miles — because the gospel is about to cross the border that mattered most.

Peter’s vision is not primarily about food. It is about people. “What God has made clean, do not call common.” The dietary laws that had kept Israel separate from the nations were always pointing toward something — a people set apart for God. Now that people is being redefined around the Messiah, and the old boundary markers are being transformed. God is not lowering his standards; he is declaring that Gentiles, received through faith in Christ, are clean. They always could be. The wall between Jew and Gentile was never in God’s ultimate plan; it was a temporary steward until the seed came (Galatians 3:24).

The Spirit falls while Peter is still preaching. Not after an altar call. Not after theological instruction is complete. The sovereign Spirit comes when and where he wills, and what he produces in the house of Cornelius is praise. The Jewish believers who came with Peter are amazed. God is not. He planned this before the foundation of the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Acts 10 is the theological center of the book. The conversion of Cornelius — a Roman centurion, a Gentile, uncircumcised — is the event that breaks open the gospel's trajectory toward the ends of the earth. Peter needs a vision from heaven before he will cross the threshold of a Gentile home; God needs to tell him three times that what he has made clean is not unclean. The resistance is not personal prejudice alone but centuries of Torah observance that drew sharp lines between Israel and the nations. To cross those lines required a direct word from God — and God gives it.

What happens in Cornelius's house is unmistakable: as Peter is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the word, and they speak in tongues and praise God. The circumcised believers who came with Peter are astonished — the Spirit has been 'poured out even on the Gentiles.' The Spirit does not wait for circumcision, for full Torah compliance, or for the completion of Peter's sermon. He falls on those who hear the word and believe, confirming that faith in Jesus Christ is the only condition of receiving the gift. This is the Gentile Pentecost, and it makes the mission to the nations not merely possible but divinely commanded.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean: The Gospel Dismantles Food Laws as Ethnic Barriers

The vision of the sheet containing all kinds of animals (vv. 9–16) uses the food laws as a symbol for the ethnic separation they enforced: if God has made all foods clean, he has made all peoples accessible. Reformed theology sees here the fulfillment of the old covenant's shadow-function: the food laws distinguished Israel from the nations as a temporary measure, pointing toward the day when the gospel would break down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–16). Cornelius's conversion is not the abandonment of God's covenant purposes but their fulfillment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter entered a Gentile home and preached the gospel, something the Torah-observant Jew in him resisted with his whole being. He needed a vision from heaven to override his cultural conditioning. Now: The church continues to need the Spirit's override of its cultural conditioning — the instinct to preach the gospel only to people like us requires the same divine interruption that Peter received.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius's characterization is carefully drawn: Roman (centurion of the Italian Cohort, a Gentile soldier), devout (a God-fearer, one who worshipped the God of Israel without full conversion), generous (almsgiving to the Jewish people), and prayerful (continually). He is the best possible Gentile from a Jewish perspective — everything that Gentile piety could be — and it is not enough. His prayers and alms are noticed by God (v. 4), but he still needs the gospel. Religious sincerity and moral generosity do not produce salvation; the gospel of Jesus Christ does.

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary: The ninth hour (3pm) is the hour of prayer in Judaism, and Cornelius is in prayer at that very hour when the angel appears. 'He stared at him in terror' — the appropriate response to a genuine divine messenger: the fear of the Lord that is the beginning of wisdom. 'Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God' — the language of the temple offering (Leviticus 2:2, 9) applied to prayer and charity: these have come before God as a fragrant offering, not in themselves salvific, but noticed and responded to by the God who hears prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's instruction is remarkably specific: not just 'find a preacher' but 'find Simon called Peter, lodging with Simon the tanner, at a house by the sea in Joppa.' God is not sending Cornelius a private revelation but directing him to a human preacher — the means of grace (the apostolic word) remains God's ordinary channel of saving faith. The specificity confirms divine orchestration: the angel knows exactly where Peter is because God has arranged the convergence. Cornelius will send men before he knows why; Peter will receive them before he knows who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having explained everything to him, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius acts immediately and completely on the angel's instruction — the mark of genuine responsiveness to God. He explains everything to his servants and the devout soldier: not just the errand but the divine context, so that those he sends understand the gravity and the source of the commission. The three men sent represent three days' journey: they will arrive at Peter's lodging on the day that God has arranged for Peter's vision to prepare him to receive them. Two divine visions are converging on a single moment of mission breakthrough.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's trance arrives in the context of prayer and hunger — the physical and spiritual combined in the moment God uses for revelation. The sixth hour (noon) and the hunger create the natural condition for what follows: a vision involving food. God's timing is sovereign even in Peter's stomach; the hunger that prompts thoughts of food prepares him to receive a vision about food laws that is actually about people. Divine revelation always meets us in the ordinary circumstances of embodied life.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The heavens opened — the same language used at Jesus's baptism (Luke 3:21) and Stephen's vision (Acts 7:56): divine initiative breaking through the boundary between heaven and earth. The sheet let down by its four corners suggests universality — the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12; Revelation 7:1), hinting that what is descending concerns the entire inhabited world. The vision arrives from above, from God, making clear that what Peter is about to hear is not human wisdom but divine revelation overriding human convention.

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All kinds of animals' — the sheet contains the full catalogue of the Levitical food lists: clean and unclean together, the comprehensive range of creatures that the Torah had divided into permitted and forbidden. 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat' — the command is direct and unambiguous, and it cuts directly across a lifetime of Torah observance. The divine voice is not asking Peter's opinion; it is issuing an instruction. The instruction is about food, but the application, Peter will discover, is about people — the food laws were always symbolic of the ethnic separation they enforced.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By no means, Lord' — the phrase contains an unresolved tension: you cannot say 'no' to someone you acknowledge as 'Lord.' Peter's resistance is genuine and deeply rooted: his entire life has been organized around these dietary boundaries, and the voice is asking him to cross them in a single moment. The tension between his acknowledgment of divine authority and his resistance to the divine command is itself the vision's point: the commandment he is most certain cannot be overridden is exactly the one God is overriding. What the Lord declares clean cannot be called common by those who follow the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'What God has made clean, do not call common' — the divine declaration overrides the Levitical categories. This is not the abrogation of God's word by a new word; it is the fulfillment of the old word by the new reality. The food laws were given to Israel to mark its distinctness from the nations; that function has been fulfilled in Christ, who is himself 'the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes' (Romans 10:4). Three times the vision is repeated — the number of confirmation, the number that Peter needs for something this radically counter-intuitive. Then it is taken up, leaving Peter to ponder. (cf. Mark 7:18–19; Col. 2:16–17)

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's perplexity is the space in which the Spirit will explain the vision. He has received a revelation from God that he cannot yet interpret; the interpretation will arrive through the three men at the gate. God's revelations often work this way: the vision precedes the understanding, the experience precedes the theology. Peter is 'pondering' — the word implies active reflection, not passive confusion. He knows something important has happened; he is working to understand what it means when the convergence of events provides the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit's explicit direction — 'I have sent them' — is the key to the chapter: the men at the gate are not random visitors but divinely dispatched messengers. 'Without hesitation' (or 'making no distinction') — the same word that Peter will use in 11:12 when he reports to Jerusalem: 'the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction.' The Spirit is removing the instinctive hesitation that Peter's cultural conditioning would produce, replacing it with the certainty that divine authorization has been given. The conversation with Cornelius is God's idea, not Peter's.
