<sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish everyone with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
The farewell at Miletus is one of the most moving passages in Acts, and the only speech Paul addresses to Christians. It is a pastor’s testament — the account of a ministry offered to its people before the man who gave it disappears from their sight. Paul did not shrink. He did not select the comfortable texts and leave the hard ones. He declared the whole counsel of God — repentance and faith, warning and promise, the cross and the coming judgment — to Jews and Greeks, in public and house to house, with tears, for three years. This is the standard.

And now he commends them to two things: God, and the word of his grace. Not to his successors. Not to an institution. Not to a programme. To God and his Word — the two sources of power that will outlast every pastor and sustain every flock. The Word that built them up will continue to build them up. The God who saved them will continue to keep them. Paul is going to Jerusalem with chains waiting; the Ephesian elders are going home to fierce wolves. Both are in the same hands.

They kneel on the beach and pray together, and then they weep — sorrowing most of all because they will not see his face again. The affection between shepherd and flock is total and mutual. This is what three years of tears and teaching and house-to-house ministry produces: a bond that no departure can finally break, because it is a bond forged in the gospel and sealed in the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third missionary journey enters its final phase as Paul turns his face toward Jerusalem. The route back — through Macedonia, Greece, and then by sea — is the reverse of the outward journey, and the pastoral quality of the narrative reflects Paul's awareness that he is saying goodbye. At Troas, the young man Eutychus falls from a window during an all-night sermon and is raised by Paul — a miracle that is also a portrait of the community gathered around the word and the table until dawn.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — apparently choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's departure from Ephesus is pastoral: he sends for the disciples and encourages them before leaving — he does not slip away in the night but says farewell, commending them to the grace of God. The journey through Macedonia is similarly characterized by 'much encouragement.' Paul is the pastor who encourages on the way out as surely as he teaches on the way in. The churches are formed not only by his arrival but by the grace of his departure.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary: The plot against Paul redirects his return route — from a direct sea voyage to Syria, he goes back overland through Macedonia. Providence works through danger: the longer route will allow him to encourage more churches and will be described in verses 4–6 with the carefully listed traveling companions who represent the collection from the Gentile churches for Jerusalem. The plot intending harm becomes an occasion for extended pastoral ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The list of companions is a catalog of the mission's fruit: delegates from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe, and Asia — representatives of churches planted on the previous two journeys. They are likely carrying the collection for Jerusalem (2 Cor. 8–9) as delegates of their churches, making this journey both a pastoral tour and an act of inter-church solidarity. The diverse roster — Macedonians, Galatians, Asians — is a living demonstration of the one body of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'we' resumes — Luke rejoins the party at Philippi, where he has apparently remained since Acts 16:17. The notation of the days of Unleavened Bread (Passover season) suggests Paul observes Jewish feasts even in Gentile contexts — not for salvation but as the rhythm of his life as a Jew who follows the Messiah. Seven days in Troas: the mission pauses to worship, break bread, and teach.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first day of the week — Sunday, the Lord's Day — is already the established day for Christian worship in this community. Breaking bread (the Lord's Supper) and the extended teaching of the word are the shape of the gathering. Paul, knowing he will depart the next morning, extends his teaching until midnight — pastoral urgency compressing all he wants to leave with them into one long night. The many lamps in the upper room create the warm, crowded scene that precedes the crisis.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's matter-of-fact candor: Eutychus falls asleep during Paul's sermon and falls from a third-story window. Luke, the physician, records him as 'taken up dead' — his clinical assessment, not a euphemism. The length of the sermon is not blamed; the young man's drowsiness is human and understandable. The miracle that follows will not make Paul's preaching briefer, but it will make the night unforgettable.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, 'Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.' And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he talked with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Elijah and Elisha parallel (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34) — bending over and embracing — marks the miracle as prophetic in character. Paul's 'do not be alarmed, his life is in him' is reassurance to the community and acknowledgment of the miracle. Then, remarkably, Paul goes back upstairs and continues the Lord's Supper and the teaching — through the night until daybreak. The resurrection of Eutychus does not end the gathering; it transforms it into an all-night celebration of life.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary: The understatement of 'not a little comforted' is characteristically Lukan — an enormous relief expressed with restrained gentleness. The community that had seen a young man fall to his death now sees him walk out alive. The miracle is not merely a wonder but a sign: the apostle of the resurrection preaches in a city where a young man is raised, and the community is comforted — literally, encouraged — as Paul had been encouraging communities throughout this entire journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul walks the twenty miles to Assos alone — a deliberate choice, perhaps for prayer and reflection as he turns toward Jerusalem. The journey south along the coast of Asia is a farewell tour of the regions where he has ministered for years. Each port is named: Mitylene, Chios, Samos, Miletus — the geography of devotion, tracing the coastline that the mission has transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we came to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be in Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul bypasses Ephesus deliberately — if he stops there he will be detained by the beloved community, and Pentecost in Jerusalem is his goal. The urgency of Jerusalem is theological, not merely sentimental: something awaits him there, and Paul senses it. He will later say he goes to Jerusalem 'compelled by the Spirit' (v. 22). But he cannot leave Asia without a word to the Ephesian elders — so he summons them to Miletus.

Is this hurry to reach Jerusalem 'on the day of Pentecost' a proof text that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part, yes — but read it carefully. It does show that Paul, himself a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast. Yet his haste was very likely as much missional as ceremonial: Pentecost packed Jerusalem with diaspora pilgrims (a prime moment to bear witness, as at the first Pentecost, Acts 2), and Paul was carrying the relief collection from the Gentile churches, which he wanted to deliver to the saints (24:17; Rom. 15:25–26). So the verse shows him honouring the festival and the Jerusalem gathering — not that he kept it as a binding law required for righteousness. (Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.)

And how does that square with Romans 7, where Paul says we 'have died to the law' (7:4–6)? It squares perfectly, once we see what 'died to the law' means. Paul is not saying the believer is now lawless, or that God's righteous will has been abolished — in the very same chapter he calls the law 'holy and righteous and good' (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master — the regime that could only accuse and curse us — so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit, not by the old written code. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost, then, is no contradiction at all: he is not under the law as a way of being justified (his justification is in Christ alone), so he is free to keep the feast — not to earn standing, but as heritage, devotion, and a bridge to his people. The fuller framework — the threefold division of the law, and the careful line between keeping a custom freely and keeping it as a requirement — is laid out at 18:18 (Paul's vow). The test there governs here too: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty. Paul hurried to Pentecost as a free man in Christ, not as a slave under law — and that is the whole difference.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders at Miletus is the most personal and theologically rich speech in Acts — the only speech in Acts addressed entirely to a Christian audience and the only extended window into Paul's understanding of his own apostolic ministry. It is also, effectively, a last will and testament: Paul does not expect to see these elders again. Three years of sustained ministry in Ephesus have produced a community and a leadership team that Paul now entrusts entirely to God and to the word of his grace.

The speech moves through three movements: retrospect (how I served among you), prospect (what awaits me in Jerusalem), and instruction (how you must serve after I am gone). Each movement is saturated with Paul's characteristic theological categories — the grace of God, the kingdom, the gospel, the blood of Christ, the Spirit's oversight of the church, the danger of wolves, the example of the minister's life. The prayer and weeping that close the scene are the expression of a depth of pastoral love that the rest of Acts rarely makes visible.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the Ephesian letters of Revelation (chapters 2–3) show a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The summons to Miletus is a pastoral act of genuine love: Paul cannot go to Ephesus, so he asks the elders to come to him. They make the roughly thirty-mile journey, and what follows is the only speech in Acts addressed exclusively to Christians — Paul's farewell to the church he loves most deeply. This is the apostle as pastor, not as missionary pioneer; the tone is intimate, retrospective, and gravely forewarning.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's ministry is summarized in three phrases: humility, tears, and trials. These are not credentials of power but marks of servanthood. The one who has raised the dead and planted churches across a continent describes his ministry as humble, tearful, and tried. This is the apostolic self-portrait: not the triumphant hero but the servant who wept over his people and endured the plots of his opponents. The tears are the measure of the love.

verseByVerse.quote: "how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, declaring to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable' — the negative formulation is deliberate: Paul is naming the temptation to withhold difficult truth from audiences who might prefer comfortable falsehood. 'Not shrinking' is the courage of the minister who loves people enough to tell them what they need to hear. 'In public and from house to house' — the complementary settings of apostolic teaching: the formal gathering and the informal domestic context. 'Repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ' — the content of three years of Ephesian ministry compressed into two words: repentance and faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul goes to Jerusalem compelled — bound, constrained — by the Spirit. He does not know the specifics, but the Spirit has been warning him through prophets in city after city: imprisonment and afflictions await. He goes not in ignorance of the danger but in submission to the Spirit despite it. This is the obedience of faith: going toward what God has called you to even when the destination is suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The most defining statement of Paul's apostolic identity: my life is not precious to me if only I can finish the course. This is not death-wish but mission-clarity — the same clarity that enabled martyrs to face death without panic. The 'ministry received from the Lord Jesus' is not Paul's career but his calling, and callings are completed in obedience, not preserved in self-protection. 'The gospel of the grace of God' — this is what the ministry is: testifying to grace. (cf. Phil. 3:13–14; 2 Tim. 4:7)

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's farewell is also his legal declaration: he is innocent of blood — Ezekiel's language for the watchman who faithfully warned (Ezek. 33). He has proclaimed the kingdom three years in Ephesus; if anyone is lost, it is not for lack of warning. His final gift to the elders: I gave you everything God gave me; your blood is not on my hands.

Notice that Paul sums up his whole three-year Ephesian ministry — to a Gentile city, in this church age — as 'proclaiming the kingdom.' Acts is framed front to back by it: the risen Jesus spent forty days 'speaking about the kingdom of God' (1:3); Philip preached 'the kingdom' to Samaritans (8:12); Paul 'reasoned and persuaded about the kingdom' at Ephesus (19:8); and the book closes with him in Rome 'proclaiming the kingdom of God' (28:31). The church-age mission is summarised, again and again, as kingdom-preaching. (For what 'the kingdom of God' means and its 'already / not yet,' see on 8:12, 14:22, Col. 1:13.)

This touches a real difference among Bible-loving Christians. Many of our dispensational brothers hesitate to link 'the kingdom' with the church at all, reserving it — especially the Davidic kingdom of the Old Testament promises — for a future, literal reign of Christ over restored national Israel in the millennium; on the classic scheme the kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected, and postponed, the present age a kind of parenthesis. Their concern is worthy and should be honoured: they want God's promises to Israel taken seriously and literally, not quietly absorbed into the church (Rom. 11 does keep a future for ethnic Israel). And the view has developed — progressive dispensationalists (Bock, Blaising) now grant the kingdom was genuinely inaugurated at Christ's exaltation (Acts 2:30–36), 'already' as well as 'not yet,' while still holding a future literal fulfilment for Israel.

From the Reformed side, the simplest point is that Scripture's own language — nowhere more than in Acts — treats the kingdom as a present reality now preached and entered, not held wholly in reserve. Believers have already been 'transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son' (Col. 1:13) and made 'a kingdom, priests to his God' (Rev. 1:6); 'the kingdom of God has come upon you,' said Jesus (Matt. 12:28). The church is not simply identical with the kingdom (God's reign is wider), but it is the kingdom's present people and outpost — those over whom King Jesus already reigns, awaiting the day it is consummated over all the earth. So you need not be shy of the word: if you belong to Christ, you already live in the kingdom, under the reign of the King — even as you pray 'your kingdom come' for its full arrival. Reformed and dispensational believers keep weighing Israel and the millennium differently; but that the King reigns now, and that his kingdom was Paul's message to the church, the text makes plain.

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The whole counsel of God' — not selected doctrines, not comfortable topics, not the parts that would be well-received. The whole. Paul's ministry in Ephesus was three years of comprehensive theological formation: the kingdom, the cross, resurrection, judgment, grace, the Holy Spirit, the life of the church. A ministry that shrinks from any part of God's counsel fails the congregation it claims to serve. Full declaration is both apostolic duty and pastoral love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock' — the order is deliberate: self-care first, because a shepherd who neglects his own soul will harm the sheep. 'Which he obtained with his own blood' — the church belongs to God because he bought it with the blood of his Son, and the preciousness of that blood is the measure of the care its overseers owe it. 'Fierce wolves' — Jesus's own word (Matt. 7:15) for false teachers who devour the flock rather than feed it: the first external threat Paul names. (cf. John 10:11–12; 1 Pet. 5:2–3)

Pause on those astonishing words: 'the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.' But God is spirit and has no blood — so how can God bleed? Only because the One who shed it, Jesus, is God. It is one of Scripture's most powerful affirmations of Christ's deity: the blood of the cross can be called God's own blood because the man who hung there is the eternal Son in our flesh (so too 'they crucified the Lord of glory,' 1 Cor. 2:8). Two things shine — the deity of your Saviour, for the cross measures how high the One who died for you truly is; and the worth of the church, a flock so precious that God bought it with his own blood. (A few manuscripts read 'church of the Lord,' and 'his own blood' could just possibly mean 'the blood of his Own [Son]'; but the plain, well-attested reading stands.)

'Made you overseers' — and you rightly sense the church struggles to find the line of what overseers should actually oversee. The words set the scope: the same men are elders (v. 17, their maturity), overseers (episkopoi, their watching over), and shepherds of the flock (v. 28). The shepherd-picture says what the oversight is: pastoral and spiritual — to feed the flock with sound teaching, guard it from wolves and error (vv. 29–30), lead it, and care for souls (Heb. 13:17). It is the care of souls by the Word, not the managing of people's private lives. (On elders' mandate, qualifications, and authority, see on 14:23.)

Now the two ditches. Overreach: Peter forbids it — elders are 'not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples' (1 Pet. 5:3); 'it shall not be so among you,' said Jesus of those who lord it over others (Matt. 20:25–26). An elder's authority is ministerial, not legislative: he applies God's Word, he does not make new laws. He is not lord of the conscience — 'God alone is Lord of the conscience' — and may not bind believers with man-made rules where Scripture is silent (the Colossian error, 'do not handle, taste, touch,' Col. 2:20–23); to police what God has left to Christian liberty (Rom. 14) is to meddle. Negligence is the opposite ditch and just as grave: Ezekiel's woe falls on shepherds who fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak or seek the straying (Ezek. 34). An elder who will not teach hard truth, stay alert to the wolves (vv. 29–31), or address serious, unrepentant sin (1 Cor. 5) has abandoned his post — and abdication dressed as 'tolerance' is no virtue.

Where, then, is the line? The Word of God: elders are firm where God is firm — on the gospel, sound doctrine, clear moral commands, the church's worship and order, grave unrepentant sin — and free where God leaves free, protecting liberty in disputable matters rather than policing it (Rom. 14:1–4). Two reminders keep the balance: the flock is not theirs but God's — they are under-shepherds of the Chief Shepherd, accountable to him (1 Pet. 5:2–4), not owners; and Paul's first word is 'pay careful attention to yourselves' — the elder who watches his own soul shepherds with the right blend of courage and gentleness. The aim throughout is the flock's good, served gladly, never for power, money, or ego (1 Pet. 5:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The internal threat — 'from among your own selves' — stands beside the external one: false teachers arise inside the community, not only outside. 'Speaking twisted things' — taking genuine truth and bending it just enough to draw people from Christ; Revelation 2–3 shows how prescient Paul's warning was. 'Three years... night and day... every one with tears' — the costly pastoral investment that earns him the right to be heard.

'Speaking twisted things' (diestrammena, bent out of shape) — and the typical 'twists' are worth seeing, because the pattern never changes. Heresy is rarely a flat denial; it is truth bent just enough to mislead, plausible and half-right (Col. 2:4). Almost every distortion does one of three things: it adds to Christ, subtracts from him, or perverts his grace. Back then: the Judaizers' legalism, adding law-keeping to Christ for salvation (Galatians; Acts 15); the proto-gnostic Colossian error — secret knowledge, angel-worship, asceticism, intermediaries crowding the Saviour (Col. 2) — also adding; the denials that subtracted — Christ's true humanity (1 John 4:2–3) or deity, and the resurrection (1 Cor. 15; 2 Tim. 2:17–18); and antinomianism, perverting grace 'into sensuality' (Jude 4; Rom. 6:1). And much was money-driven, 'teaching for shameful gain' (Titus 1:11; 1 Tim. 6:5).

Today the same three twists wear new clothes. Adding: the prosperity gospel, promising health and wealth to enough faith or giving — the old money-driven error in a fresh suit; and the perennial legalism that makes rules the measure of acceptance (Col. 2:16). Subtracting: the liberal emptying of the faith — denying Christ's deity, the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, the atonement, Scripture's authority; 'moralistic therapeutic deism,' a tame God who exists to make you comfortable, sin and cross quietly removed; and the universalism that twists 'God is love' into 'all paths lead home.' Perverting grace: 'cheap grace' and 'hyper-grace' that drop repentance and holiness. And mark the tell-tale motive Paul names — teachers who arise 'to draw away the disciples after them': the cult of personality, a following gathered around a man, not the Lord. So your test (the Berean way, 17:11): does this teaching exalt Christ and humble me, or exalt the teacher and serve his crowd and his wallet? Does it add to Christ, subtract from him, or turn grace into licence? Hold fast to the Head (Col. 2:19) and let the Word dwell richly (Col. 3:16); a heart full of the real Christ is not easily sold a counterfeit.

And what was Paul admonishing them about, 'night and day for three years, with tears'? The word (noutheteō) means to warn and earnestly counsel, and chiefly he was guarding them from exactly these twisted teachers (vv. 29–30), pleading with each to hold fast to Christ. But it was wider — he had 'not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God' (v. 27): sin and judgment, repentance and holiness, the cross, the suffering on the road into the kingdom (14:22). Why the tears? Because souls and eternity were at stake, and Paul loved these people. Real pastoral love is never bland; it warns, and warns weeping — 'I tell you even with tears' (Phil. 3:18). Notice how the tears answer both ditches of v. 28: no negligent shepherd (he warned relentlessly), yet no domineering one (he warned with tears, not contempt) — the model for every parent, friend, and elder who must one day say a hard word: warn, yes, but with a breaking heart for the one you love.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's benediction: he commends them not to programs or strategies but to God and to the word of his grace. The word is able — able to build up, able to give the inheritance. When Paul is gone, the word remains. The church is not dependent on its founding apostle but on the apostolic word that he has fully declared. The disclaimer about silver and gold follows naturally: he has not ministered for personal gain, and his successor ministers — the elders — must embody the same financial disinterestedness.

Four phrases, briefly. 'I commend you to God and to the word of his grace.' 'Commend' (paratithēmi) means to entrust, to hand over for safekeeping, like leaving a treasure in trusted hands. Paul is going and will not return, so he deposits the elders with two keepers who never leave: God himself, and 'the word of his grace' (the gospel, the message of God's grace, 20:24). The flock is not left orphaned — the under-shepherd departs, but the Chief Shepherd remains, and his word abides. The church's security never rested on Paul; it rests on God and his Word.

'Able to build you up.' 'Build up' (oikodomeo) is the construction word — to strengthen, mature, and establish. Notice the power lies in the word: the gospel is not lifeless information but a living means by which God grows his people strong (1 Pet. 2:2; recall 19:20, 'the word increased'). So how does a church grow after even a great leader is gone? By the word of grace, fed on and held fast. 'Give you the inheritance.' The same word that builds them up now also secures their future: a share in the eternal inheritance — the full glory of salvation, the kingdom, eternal life (as Col. 1:12, 'the inheritance of the saints in light'; 1 Pet. 1:4). And it is an inheritance, not a wage — given to children by grace, received by being in Christ, not earned.

'Among all those who are sanctified.' 'Sanctified' (hagiazo, to make holy, set apart for God) here is a perfect passive — 'those who have been sanctified' — so it describes a settled standing, not an achievement: it means simply all true believers, everyone whom God has set apart for himself in Christ (the 'saints'; cf. 1 Cor. 6:11, 'you were sanctified'; Heb. 10:10). The inheritance is not for an elite who have made themselves holy enough, but for all whom God has made holy — and the believer receives his portion together with the whole company of the saved. The comfort is rich: when every human helper is gone, God and his gospel remain — strong enough to grow you now, and faithful enough to bring you home to the inheritance at the last, in the company of all the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's hands — the tentmaker's calloused hands — are the evidence of his integrity. He worked with them not only to support himself but to model the generosity that the gospel requires. 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' is a saying of Jesus not recorded in the four Gospels — one of the few such sayings preserved in Acts. The apostle who could have been supported by the churches chose to work so that he could give. This is the economic ethics of the kingdom made visible in a life. (cf. Luke 6:38; 2 Cor. 9:7)

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The farewell is physical and communal: kneeling, prayer, tears, embracing, kissing. The emotional intensity Luke records is not sentimentality but the depth of apostolic love and communal grief. These elders have been formed by three years of Paul's teaching and pastoral care; they are losing their father in the faith. The tears are evidence that genuine pastoral ministry creates genuine bonds of love — and genuine grief at parting.

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary: The specific cause of the deepest sorrow: his word that they would not see his face again. The community's grief is not generic but anchored to a specific loss — the presence of the man who has shaped their souls. They accompany him to the ship: even the farewell is extended, prolonged, reluctant to end. The journey to Jerusalem begins from this shore of tears, and Paul goes toward suffering carried by the love of those who cannot follow.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God and Pastoral Faithfulness. Acts 20:27 gives the church its standard for preaching: the whole counsel of God, without shrinking. This phrase has defined the Reformed tradition’s commitment to expository, systematic, comprehensive proclamation of Scripture — preaching through whole books, teaching the full range of doctrine, refusing to select only the comfortable and suppress the challenging. The shepherd who preaches the whole counsel will declare both the tenderness of the Father and the terror of the Judge, both the free grace of justification and the necessary fruit of sanctification, both the comfort of election and the urgency of repentance. Paul could stand before his people at Miletus and say “I am innocent of your blood” because he had given them everything. That is the standard every preacher must aspire to.
20.examples:
Then: A beach at Miletus, a group of weeping elders on their knees, a man who knew he was going to chains and possibly death — and who spent his last hours with these people not arranging his escape but commending them to God and declaring his conscience clear. The tears on the beach are the overflow of three years of tears in the houses of Ephesus. Ministry that produces this kind of grief at parting has been ministry that produced this kind of love in the doing.

Now: Paul’s farewell is the standard against which every pastoral ministry will be measured. Did we shrink? Did we select? Did we give them the comfortable Christ without the demanding Lord, the free grace without the costly discipleship, the promise without the warning? The whole counsel of God. Nothing less. The flock that has been given the whole counsel will be able to stand when the wolves come — because they will recognise the deviation when they hear it.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own hands and feet and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed. They are all zealous for the law. <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple and stirred up all the crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>36</sup>For the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”
21.overview:
The journey to Jerusalem is a journey into known suffering. At every stop, the Spirit witnesses that chains and afflictions await. At Tyre, disciples urge Paul not to go. At Caesarea, Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and delivers the Spirit’s message with prophetic theatre: this is what Jerusalem will do to the man who owns this belt. Everyone weeps. Everyone pleads. And Paul, unmoved, asks why they are breaking his heart.

He is not reckless. He is not looking for martyrdom. He is constrained by the Spirit — the same Spirit whose warnings he hears and receives, and who nevertheless calls him forward. The will of the Lord leads into suffering. And Paul’s companions, when they cannot dissuade him, say the only thing that remains: “Let the will of the Lord be done.” This is not resignation; it is the profound submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are not derailed by human suffering — they are often advanced through it.

Jerusalem receives Paul with joy — James and the elders glorify God over the Gentile mission. But within days the Asian Jews see Paul in the temple and the city erupts. He is dragged out, beaten, on the verge of death, and saved by Roman soldiers. As they carry him up the steps of the barracks, the crowd shouting “away with him” below, Paul asks the tribune for permission to speak. The prisoner wants to preach. He is not finished yet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final journey to Jerusalem is framed by a series of increasingly urgent warnings: at Tyre, the disciples 'through the Spirit' tell Paul not to go to Jerusalem; at Caesarea, Agabus the prophet binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and declares that the Jews in Jerusalem will bind him just like this. The community's response is weeping, imploring Paul not to go. Paul's response is the response of Gethsemane: 'What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.' The community relents: 'The will of the Lord be done.'
verseByVerse.theology:
The Will of the Lord and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Caesarean community's submission to 'the will of the Lord be done' after every argument against Paul's Jerusalem journey is one of the most powerful statements of Christian relinquishment in Acts. They cannot change Paul's mind; they cannot change what the Spirit has revealed awaits him; all they can do is yield to the will of the Lord whose purposes exceed their understanding. Reformed theology sees here the Christian response to suffering that cannot be avoided: not stoic resignation but active trust, the 'Nevertheless, not my will but yours' of Gethsemane repeated in every generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul went to Jerusalem knowing imprisonment awaited him, because the Spirit had told him to go. Obedience to the Spirit's direction sometimes leads toward suffering, not away from it. Now: The willingness to walk toward the suffering the Spirit assigns, rather than away from it, is the defining characteristic of the cross-shaped life that Paul modeled and calls his communities to follow.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'we' continues as the company sails south and east toward Jerusalem. The journey is described with the precision of a ship's log: Cos, Rhodes, Patara — the named ports mark the finality of the departure. Each port left behind is another step away from the churches of the Aegean mission and toward the Jerusalem that awaits. The directness of the route — 'by a straight course' — suggests favorable winds and providential guidance toward what Paul knows will be suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary: Cyprus on the left — the island where the first missionary journey began, where Barnabas's home church was, now passed without stopping. The mission has moved beyond its first geographic horizons. Tyre, the ancient Phoenician port city, is the stopover point, and it will yield an unexpected and significant prophetic encounter while the ship unloads.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Tyrian disciples warn Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem — a warning similar to what awaits in Caesarea. Paul does not disobey the Spirit; he discerns that the Spirit's testimony about coming suffering does not constitute a prohibition on going. The call to Jerusalem and the warning of suffering come from the same Spirit. The farewell at the beach — kneeling in prayer with the whole community, wives and children — mirrors the Miletus farewell. The journey to the cross has its own stations of communal love.

verseByVerse.quote: "and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home."
verseByVerse.commentary: The simplicity of the parting: farewells exchanged, the ship boarded, the community returning home. Luke's restraint here is eloquent — the tenderness of the beach prayer is followed by the quiet finality of departure. Paul does not look back. The mission has its own momentum, its own obedience, its own trajectory toward Jerusalem and ultimately Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip the evangelist — one of the Seven deacons appointed in Acts 6, the one who preached to the Samaritans and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch — has a home and family in Caesarea. Decades have passed since those early events; Philip is now a settled figure with daughters who prophesy. The mission's history is embodied in living people: Philip connects the reader back to the earliest chapters of Acts while standing in its final movement.

verseByVerse.quote: "He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied."
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip's four daughters are prophets — women exercising the gift of prophecy in the early church, fulfilling Joel's promise (Acts 2:17–18) that God's Spirit would be poured out on sons and daughters alike. They are unmarried, perhaps devoted entirely to their prophetic ministry. Luke mentions them briefly but significantly: the Spirit distributes gifts as he wills, without regard to gender. Their prophetic presence is part of the texture of the Spirit-filled community that Paul encounters on his way to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul's belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit, "This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Agabus — who previously prophesied the famine (Acts 11:28) — enacts the prophecy with dramatic, prophetic symbolism in the tradition of the Hebrew prophets (Jeremiah and Ezekiel used similar acted signs). The belt-binding is visual and visceral: this is how Paul will be bound. The prophecy is specific about the agents — the Jews bind him and deliver him to the Gentiles — a pattern that echoes the passion of Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary: The community's response — including Luke ('we') and the Caesarean believers — is to urge Paul not to go. The warning is now universal: disciples in Tyre, Agabus in Caesarea, the 'we' company, the whole community. And Paul will not be dissuaded. This is not stubbornness but submission: he has heard the Spirit's testimony, acknowledged the suffering that awaits, and chosen obedience over self-preservation. The community's love for him is genuine, and he receives it; but it cannot redirect him from what the Lord has called him to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "The will of the Lord be done."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You are breaking my heart' — Paul is not unmoved by the weeping; the grief touches him deeply. But the readiness to be imprisoned and to die cannot be argued away by tears: it is itself the Spirit's gift to the one who has been told what awaits. 'I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die' — the freedom from the fear of death that Paul has been teaching throughout his ministry is now his own lived reality at its most costly. 'The will of the Lord be done' — the community's submission is the Gethsemane prayer of the church: yielding to what they cannot change and trusting the Lord whose will it is. (cf. Luke 22:42; Phil. 1:20–21)

verseByVerse.quote: After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.
verseByVerse.commentary: The company that makes the final journey to Jerusalem is substantial: the travel companions from multiple Gentile churches, Luke, some Caesarean disciples, and a welcome lodging with Mnason — 'an early disciple,' one of the first generation of believers in Cyprus, perhaps known to Barnabas who was also Cypriot. The detail of Mnason grounds the arrival in the web of personal relationships that the gospel has been weaving across the Mediterranean world. The first generation of disciples is still alive in Jerusalem; Paul arrives not as a stranger but as one returning to the community from which everything began.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's arrival in Jerusalem triggers a sequence of events that will occupy the rest of Acts. The initial welcome by the Jerusalem elders under James's leadership is warm; the problem is the report about Paul that has been circulating among Jewish believers: that he teaches Jews in the Diaspora to abandon Moses, circumcision, and the customs. James proposes a practical solution — Paul joining four men in a Nazirite purification vow, demonstrating that he himself lives in observance of the law — designed to show Jewish believers that Paul's practice is not what the rumors say.

The plan almost works. But Paul is spotted in the temple by Jews from Asia who have seen him with Trophimus the Ephesian and assume he has brought a Gentile into the temple courts (a capital offense). The riot that follows requires Roman military intervention: the tribune Claudius Lysias rescues Paul from the mob, arrests him in chains, and allows him to address the crowd from the steps of the Antonia Fortress — setting up the speech of chapter 22 and the long legal process that will carry Paul to Rome.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom in Accommodation and the Line That Cannot Be Crossed

Paul's willingness to participate in the Nazirite vow is the pastoral wisdom of 1 Corinthians 9: becoming all things to all people for the sake of the gospel. The line that cannot be crossed is the line of the gospel itself: adding circumcision as a condition of Gentile salvation (Galatians 5:2). The Nazirite vow does not cross that line; it is a voluntary act of cultural accommodation by a free man, not a requirement imposed on Gentile converts. The distinction between voluntary accommodation and imposed requirement is the line Reformed missiology must maintain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was rescued from a lynching by Roman soldiers and given the opportunity to address the crowd from the barracks steps. The Roman captivity that will carry him to Rome begins with a rescue, not an arrest. Providence uses the empire's order to preserve the witness the empire will eventually hear. Now: God continues to use the structures of civil authority — sometimes surprisingly — to protect the gospel's proclamation and to bring the witness to unexpected places.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jerusalem receives them gladly — the community of believers in the holy city welcomes the missionary band. The formal meeting is with James and all the elders of the Jerusalem church. This is the established leadership pattern: James presides, the elders are present, the apostolic missionary reports. Paul has traveled to Jerusalem carrying the collection from the Gentile churches and the fruit of years of mission — he brings both as offerings to the mother church.

verseByVerse.quote: "After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed. They are all zealous for the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's mission report is received with worship: they glorified God. The pattern from Acts 15 repeats — the testimony of what God has done among the Gentiles produces doxology. But then the elders immediately present their own concern: many thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem, all zealous for the law, and rumors that Paul has been teaching Jews in the diaspora to forsake Moses. The tension between Jewish and Gentile Christianity, settled in principle at Jerusalem, remains alive in practice.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or to walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rumor about Paul is a distortion: he teaches that Gentiles need not be circumcised, but he has not taught Jews to forsake Moses (as Timothy's circumcision in Acts 16 demonstrates). The elders know Paul is innocent of the charge but understand that his presence in Jerusalem will trigger the assumption of guilt. They propose a solution that will demonstrate publicly what they know to be true about Paul's practice.

Was the rumour true? Honestly, the right answer is: partly, in a sense — but as stated, no. It is worth seeing both halves. What was false: Paul never taught Jews to 'forsake Moses' or to stop circumcising their children. He kept the customs himself, freely and gladly — he took a Nazirite vow (18:18), circumcised Timothy (16:3), hurried to keep Pentecost (20:16), worshipped in the temple, and is about to join four men in their vow precisely to show it (vv. 23–26). The word in the charge is apostasy (rebellion, abandonment), and of that Paul was simply innocent; he honoured his heritage and called the law 'holy and righteous and good' (Rom. 7:12).

But here is the kernel of truth that made the rumour believable. Paul really did teach something radical: that nothing — not circumcision, not law-keeping — makes anyone right with God; that justification is by faith in Christ alone (Galatians; Romans); that Gentile believers need not keep the law at all (Acts 15; he refused to circumcise Titus, Gal. 2:3–5); that the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Col. 2:16–17); and that the believer has 'died to the law' as a way of standing before God (Rom. 7:4–6). In short, he taught that the customs are not required and not binding, and that they count for nothing as the ground of salvation. It is not hard to see how, in the heat of controversy and hostile retelling, that got stretched into 'Paul tells everyone to forsake Moses.' The rumour took 'you are free from the law' and twisted it into 'you must abandon the law' — and that gap is the whole point. Paul preached freedom, not apostasy: a Jewish believer is free to keep his customs as heritage and witness, free not to, and never to trust them for salvation. (See the fuller framework at 18:18 and 20:16.)

So the lesson is twofold. First, see how easily a faithful teacher's true message is distorted by exaggeration — 'the law saves no one and binds no Gentile' becomes 'he hates Moses' (the same kind of 'twisting' Paul warned of in 20:30). And second, watch Paul's response: he will gladly use his liberty to live as a Jew among Jews, to disarm the slander and win his people (1 Cor. 9:20), without surrendering one inch of the gospel that the law cannot save. Free enough to keep the custom; too faithful to ever make it a requirement.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proposal is pragmatic and pastoral: Paul sponsors four men completing a Nazirite vow, participating in the purification rites, publicly demonstrating his continued practice of Jewish customs. This is the same principle as Timothy's circumcision — Paul accommodates Jewish practice when the gospel is not at stake, to remove unnecessary barriers to his witness. He is willing to be seen in the temple fulfilling the law's requirements, not to earn righteousness but to make clear that following Jesus does not require apostasy from Israel.

The Nazirite vow (Numbers 6) is worth explaining, since the practice is entirely foreign to us today. A Nazirite vow was a voluntary dedication to the LORD for a set period. It involved three abstentions: (1) no wine, grape products, or fermented drink — even grape juice or raisins were forbidden; (2) no razor to the head — the uncut hair was the visible sign of consecration, accumulating throughout the vow period; (3) no contact with a corpse, even that of a parent or sibling — a stricter purity requirement than even the high priest's. At the vow's completion, the Nazirite went to the temple, brought prescribed offerings (burnt offering, sin offering, peace offering, grain offering), had his head shaved, and the hair was burned on the altar. The entire process was costly in time, money, and public visibility. Paul 'paying their expenses' means funding the required offerings — an act of considerable financial generosity that visibly placed him in the company of faithful Jewish Christians fulfilling their vows. The sponsorship was a recognized form of Jewish piety in the Second Temple period (attested in 1 Maccabees and Josephus) and would have carried unmistakable meaning to any Jerusalem observer.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality." Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification, when the offering would be made for each one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James's reminder of the Jerusalem Council decree ('we have sent a letter') reaffirms that the Gentile requirements have not changed: the four abstentions that protect Jewish-Gentile fellowship are the only requirements placed on Gentile believers. Paul's acceptance of the plan and his entry into the temple with the four men is the pastoral accommodation in action: free from the law, freely choosing to observe it for the sake of the Jerusalem community's peace. The offering he arranges for each of the four men is expensive — another practical demonstration that he is not teaching against the law's observance among Jewish believers.

(On why these four things were asked of Gentile believers — not as law for salvation, but for the sake of love and table-fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians, and to keep new converts clear of pagan idolatry — see the full explanation at the Jerusalem Council, 15:19–20, which also shows how it harmonises with Paul's later teaching on food offered to idols in 1 Corinthians.)

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The accusation is false: they have seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and assume he brought him into the temple — but assumption is enough to ignite a riot. 'Teaching against the people, the law, and this place' echoes the charges against Stephen in Acts 6. Paul is entering the same passion narrative that his predecessor Stephen entered. The Jerusalem temple is the flashpoint; the charge is defilement of the sacred; the mob's violence is immediate.

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary: The gate-shutting is both practical (keeping the Gentile from further contaminating the sacred space) and symbolic: Paul is excluded from the temple he has honored, on a false charge, by his own people. The doors shut behind him are the doors of the old covenant order shutting on the apostle of the new. He will never enter the temple again. The arrest on a false charge, the violence of the crowd, the dragging out — these are the passion's echo in the apostle's life.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Roman tribune — the commander of the cohort garrisoned in the Antonia Fortress adjacent to the temple — intervenes to save Paul's life. Roman soldiers descend the steps into the outer court; the mob stops beating Paul. The irony is complete: the Roman military, which Paul's accusers say he has offended by bringing a Gentile into the temple, is the instrument of his deliverance from the mob. Rome saves Paul from Jerusalem — repeatedly, throughout the rest of Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary: The binding with two chains fulfills Agabus's prophecy literally. Paul is now a prisoner of Rome — which will prove, paradoxically, to be the vehicle by which he reaches Caesar's household and eventually Rome itself. The tribune's inquiry — who is he, what has he done? — is the beginning of the legal process that will occupy the remaining chapters of Acts. Paul will use every legal proceeding as an opportunity to proclaim the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The chaos mirrors the Ephesian riot: the crowd shouting contradictory things, the tribune unable to learn anything from the uproar, the soldiers having to carry Paul up the steps. The violence of the crowd is such that Paul cannot walk — he is physically overwhelmed. The barracks of the Antonia Fortress will be his first Roman custody, and it will immediately become a preaching platform.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Away with him!' — the same cry that greeted Jesus before Pilate (Luke 23:18). Paul's passion mirrors his Lord's: accused by his own people, handed to the Gentiles, cried against by the mob. Luke's echo is deliberate and theological: the servant is not above his master, and the apostle of the crucified one follows the pattern of the cross. The journey to Jerusalem has reached its destination; the journey to Rome is about to begin.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The tribune mistakes Paul for a notorious Egyptian revolutionary who had led a messianic movement to the Mount of Olives — a movement the Romans had recently suppressed violently. That an educated, Greek-speaking man is in Roman custody after a temple riot is enough to suggest this identification. Paul's fluent Greek immediately signals that he is someone else entirely — someone educated, someone with standing, someone whose story the tribune has not yet heard.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's self-identification is carefully calibrated: Tarsus, no obscure city, known for its philosophical culture. But his request is not for sympathy or legal protection — he wants to speak to the people who have just tried to kill him. The permission is granted; he stands on the steps of the Antonia above the crowd; he motions for silence, and the crowd hushed. He will speak to them in Hebrew — Aramaic — the language of their hearts, and what he says will be his own conversion testimony: the most powerful apologetic a man can give.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 presents with unusual clarity the Reformed conviction that the will of God is not always comfortable, and that knowing it does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await. He goes anyway. His companions know Paul knows. They submit anyway. “Let the will of the Lord be done” is not fatalism — it is the active, willing submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are worked out through suffering, not around it. This is the theology of Romans 8:28 embodied in a house in Caesarea: all things — including imprisonment, beatings, and the howling of a mob — work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Paul’s chains will take him to Rome. God knew this. Paul submitted to it. Rome receives the gospel.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, accompanied by weeping friends who have said everything they can say and now can only pray. A church in Jerusalem that receives the Gentile mission report with joy and then watches its guest arrested in the temple court. The will of the Lord, being done — at great cost, with great grief, toward a great purpose that none of them can yet see fully.

Now: The church in every age must learn the grammar of “let the will of the Lord be done.” It is learned most deeply in the moments when the will of the Lord leads into what we would not choose — illness, loss, rejection, persecution. Paul goes to Jerusalem not because it is easy or because he can see the outcome, but because the Spirit has said go and the Lord has said trust. This is the faith that follows a Lord who himself prayed “not my will, but yours.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Standing on the steps of the Antonia Fortress above the crowd that has just tried to kill him, Paul speaks in Aramaic — the language of their hearts — and tells the story of his life. This is not merely autobiography; it is theology embodied in a testimony. Paul was once exactly where his accusers are: zealous for the law, convinced that Jesus was a threat to Israel, persecuting the church with the approval of the high priest. What changed him was not argument but encounter — the risen Jesus on the Damascus road. The speech is a masterclass in contextual proclamation: Paul meets his audience on their own ground, in their own language, with their own categories, and leads them to the one thing they cannot accept: that the God of their fathers has sent him to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul's conversion testimony is itself a theological argument. He was not a pagan converted to a new religion; he was a zealous Jew transformed by the risen Messiah of Israel. His call to the Gentiles is not betrayal of Judaism but fulfillment of Israel's prophetic vocation — to be a light to the nations. The missionary call comes from Ananias, a devout Jew, and is confirmed by a vision in the temple itself. The God who spoke to Abraham, Moses, and the prophets is the God who spoke to Paul on the Damascus road.
verseByVerse.examples: Reformed preachers have long used Paul's conversion as a model for presenting the gospel to those who are religious but unregenerate. Keller notes that Paul does not attack Jewish religion but shows how it is fulfilled in Christ. Calvin observes that the testimony of a former persecutor is among the most powerful arguments for the resurrection: only a genuine encounter with the risen Christ can explain the transformation of the chief enemy of the church into its chief apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Brothers and fathers' — Paul addresses the crowd with the familial language of a fellow Jew, not the defensive posture of an accused outsider. The Aramaic creates an immediate, unexpected bond: the man they have been trying to kill speaks their native tongue with evident fluency. The hush that falls is the gospel's opening — a moment of genuine attention purchased by the familiarity of the language. Paul has been given a platform he could not have manufactured, on the steps of Rome's fortress, by the providence of the riot itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's credentials are impeccable and his audience knows it: Tarsus-born but Jerusalem-educated, Gamaliel's student — the greatest rabbi of the generation — trained according to the strictest interpretation of Torah, zealous for God as they are zealous. And he persecuted the Way to the death. He is not defending himself against a charge of abandoning Judaism; he is presenting himself as someone whose Judaism was more rigorous than most of theirs before the risen Christ redirected it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The high priest and the council as character witnesses — Paul's persecution of the church was authorized at the highest levels of Jewish authority. He is not a renegade from the margins but the official instrument of mainstream Judaism's opposition to the Way. 'About noon a great light from heaven' — the midday sun is already blazing, and this light outshines it. The risen Christ appears in glory that surpasses the brightest natural light: the light of the world revealing himself at noon.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The name — 'Jesus of Nazareth' — is everything. This is not a generic divine vision but the specific person Paul has been hunting: the crucified rabbi from Galilee. The identification of Jesus with his persecuted followers — 'why are you persecuting me?' — reveals the theology of the body of Christ: to persecute the church is to persecute Jesus himself. The one Paul thought was a dangerous imposter turns out to be the Lord of glory, and the persecution of his followers is a direct assault on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'What shall I do, Lord?' — the first question of Paul's new life. The one who had known exactly what to do — persecute the Way — now has no program, no agenda, no certainty but the voice. Conversion is always this: the dissolution of the self-constructed program and the surrender to the Lord's direction. The answer is deliberately incomplete: go to Damascus, and there you will be told. Not the full plan, only the next step. This is how the Lord leads.

Was Paul already born again at this point? The honest answer is that we are not told, and we should not pretend to know what Scripture does not say. Luke narrates Paul's conversion as a connected whole — the blinding encounter on the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16) — without putting a stopwatch on the exact instant of the new birth. That should not surprise us: regeneration is the Spirit's secret, invisible work, known with certainty only to God; we never observe the moment itself, only its fruits.

What we can observe is suggestive. By v. 10 Paul calls Jesus 'Lord,' surrenders his whole program, asks 'what shall I do?', obeys, and then spends three days in prayer (9:11, 'behold, he is praying') — all marks of a heart already being turned to Christ. And from a Reformed vantage, since the new birth is what produces faith and repentance, it is reasonable to think the Spirit's regenerating work was already underlying that genuine submission. But we hold this loosely, because the same account locates the gift of the Spirit at Ananias's coming, and has Ananias say, 'rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name' (22:16) — language that warns us against fixing the moment too precisely. So: it is fair to say a converting work was plainly under way by v. 10; it is not fair to claim the text dates the new birth to this verse. We simply do not know the instant.

And here is the comfort in the honest uncertainty: what Scripture leaves unclear (the when) it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear (the who). From first to last this is sovereign grace — Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul. The exact timing of the new birth is God's secret; the source of it is no secret at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, came to me,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Ananias is introduced with care before Agrippa: devout, according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews — a thoroughly Jewish figure, not a pagan convert. Paul is not received into a new religion by an outsider; he is received by a faithful Jew into the fulfillment of Israel's Messiah. The blinding that has brought him by hand into Damascus is the darkness from which Ananias's coming will deliver him — spiritually as well as physically.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Brother Saul' — the first time Paul is addressed as brother by a believer. The address acknowledges him as a member of the family of faith before he has been baptized, before he has had time to prove himself. This is grace: the community receives the former persecutor as a brother because the risen Christ has already claimed him. The restored sight is both physical and spiritual; the one who has been blinded by his own righteousness now sees.
